# Deadliest Mountains In The World

May 5

Written By [Makura Creations](https://www.namasadventure.com/7000m-8000mexpeditions-blog-posts?author=69856005fba77c419ceb5ad8)

[![Image 7](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/55d729cfe4b00ab3960e7989/c259fee4-ea6a-469e-a8e4-b63ca7907c8d/Annapurna+1+expedition+20.jpg)](https://www.namasadventure.com/annapurna-1-8091m-expedition)

Mount Everest

When we talk about the **deadliest mountains on earth**, most people believe Mount Everest is the one. But in reality, it is not true. While [**Mount Everest (8,848.86 m)**](https://www.namasadventure.com/everest-expedition-8849-nepal-himalayas) is the highest mountain in the world, it is not as deadly as mountains like **Annapurna I (8,091m)**, **K2 (8,611m)**, **Nanga Parbat (8,126 m),** and others.

Deadliest mountains are calculated by measuring their **fatality rate**, which is the ratio of climber deaths to successful summit attempts. The altitude, weather, and terrain conditions of mountains increase the death rates and deadliness of the mountains.

In this blog, we provide information about the **deadliest mountains in the world** that claimed the lives of many climbers on the basis of fatality rate. Also, the factor making mountains deadly and why such mountains kill during descents is also explained.

## What Makes a Mountain Deadly?

Mountains are deadly when they combine life-threatening situations like difficult terrain, high altitude, unpredictable weather, and strong jet winds. These situations challenge climbers at every point and claim their lives. Some of the key factors that make mountains deadly include the following:

*   **High altitude:** The high altitude of the mountain makes it deadly due to limited oxygen, altitude sickness, and an increased chance of exhaustion.

*   **Avalanches:**Avalanches are the key factor that makes mountains deadly. They occur when large masses of ice, snow, and debris slide down below mountains. Avalanches occur without obvious warning and increase risks due to rapid asphyxiation, blunt force trauma, and hypothermia. Most deaths occur due to suffocation and pressure of massive weight when buried.

*   **Rock Fall:** Rock falls are a common cause of deaths where loose rocks fall from steep mountains and collide with climbers. The heavy rocks falling from a distance at high speed are unpredictable and highly unavoidable during steep climbing. If they hit climbers, they cause serious injuries or even deaths.

*   **Unpredictable weather:**Unpredictable weather or the sudden change in weather challenges climbers. The freezing temperature, strong jet winds, and snowstorm increase the chance of fatalities.

*   **Terrain:** The terrain or slope of the mountain also makes it challenging and deadly. Steep slopes and challenging terrain requiring technical skills increase exhaustion, the chance of accidents, and injuries leading to fatalities.

*   **Crevasses:** Crevasses are deep cracks on mountains that trap mountaineers if they accidentally step on the gap. The increased number of hidden crevasses in the mountain increases the risk and mortality rate in the mountain.

**Remote locations:** The remote altitude and location of the mountains make it difficult to conduct rescue operations. These increase the risk that claims the lives of mountaineers, making the mountain deadly.

## Deadliest Mountains in the World

| Mountain | Height | Location | Main Deadly Factor |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Annapurna I** | 8,091 m | Nepal | Altitude, avalanches, and unstable slopes |
| **K2** | 8,611 m | Pakistan/China | Altitude, technical climbing difficulty, and deadly storms |
| **Nanga Parbat** | 8,126 m | Pakistan | High altitude, rockfalls, and extreme weather |
| **Kangchenjunga** | 8,586 m | Nepal/India | Remote terrain, high altitude, and heavy snowfall |
| **Dhaulagiri I** | 8,167 m | Nepal | Avalanche risk, steep vertical gain, and high altitude |

### Annapurna I (8,091m)

![Image 8](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/55d729cfe4b00ab3960e7989/20edbb23-3bc8-4d15-83cd-c8ad006fd53f/Annapurna+1+expedition+8.jpg)

Annapurna I

The [**Annapurna I (8,091 m)**](https://www.namasadventure.com/annapurna-1-8091m-expedition) is one of the deadliest mountains in the world, with a 20% to 32% fatality rate. It is located in the Himalayas in Nepal and is**the 10th highest mountain in the world**.

Annapurna I's unpredictability, risk of avalanche, poor weather, terrain condition, and altitude have claimed the lives of many climbers. The entire mountain is considered highly risky with snowy slopes and hazard concentrations. Annapurna I’s vertical geography, hanging seracs, and hard blue ice act as factors that trigger avalanches.

While more than 365 climbers reach the summit of Annapurna I, 72 people have been recorded to have been killed in an attempt to climb Annapurna I.

### K2 (8,611m)

[K2 (8,611m)](https://www.namasadventure.com/mount-k2-expedition)is the **world's second-highest mountain**, located on the border of China and Pakistan. The K2 is located in the Karakoram range and is also known as “**The Savage Mountain."**It is one of the deadliest mountains in the world due to its technical 60 degree ice traverse beneath the unstable serac at an altitude of 8,200 m.

The technical challenges due to steep slopes, loose rocks, and the remote location of the mountain make it even deadlier. Its route involves vertical broken rock faces that fall down directly below the narrow paths that climbers pass through. The rocks acting as shooting galleries increase risk to climbers.

K2 held a death rate of 4:1 prior to 2021. While 800 climbers have submitted K2 successfully, 96 deaths have been reported during the attempt.

### Nanga Parbat (8,126 m)

Nanga Parbat is the world's ninth highest mountain, located in the Pakistan-administered region of Gilgit-Baltistan. It is also known as “**Killer Mountain”** due to a fatality rate of 20 % to 22%.

As of August 2023, a total of 96 fatalities are recorded in 800 successful summits. The technical difficulty, unpredictable weather, high risk of avalanche, and difficult descent route make Nanga Parbat the deadliest mountain in the world.

Also, the **risk of rockfall is high in Nanga Parbat** due to the presence of fractured rocks and unstable surfaces leading to frequent rockfall. Many climbers have reported rockfall as constant and challenging when climbing Nanga Parbat.

### Kanchenjunga (8,586 m)

Kanchenjunga is the **world’s third-highest pea**k, standing tall at an altitude of 8,586 m on the border of Nepal and India. It is also referred to as “**The Five Treasures of the Great Snow**” and is known for being one of the deadliest mountains in the world.

The fatality rate of Kanchenjunga climbers is high, as it crosses 20% in an attempt to summit the main peak. While mountaineering equipment, techniques, and well-planned adventures are practiced, more than 52 climbers have been reported to have lost their lives till May 2022.

Meanwhile, the successful summit number recorded is 532. The remote location, high altitude, constant avalanches, long routes, and extreme difficulty.

### Dhaulagiri I (8,167m)

[![Image 9](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/55d729cfe4b00ab3960e7989/be21c7bf-631c-446e-bcbb-16c0c3d5f1cb/49000469136_8cac32c80f_o.jpg)](https://www.namasadventure.com/dhaulagiri-8167m-expedition)

Dhaulagiri 8167m

[Dhaulagiri (8,167 m)](https://www.namasadventure.com/dhaulagiri-8167m-expedition) is the world's 7th highest mountain, located in Gandaki river basin in Nepal. It is also referred to as “**beautiful white mountain."**Although Dhqaulagiri is referred to as beautiful, it has claimed the lives of many climbers who dared to reach its summit.

Its extreme weather, technical difficulty, and risk of avalanche are killer aspects of the mountain. Also, the steep vertical gain from base camp and strong high-altitude wind further challenge the mountaineer.

The death rate of Dhaulagiri is 6.2% as of 2007 where 58 fatalities were recorded in 358 successful summits. In the latest incident of 2024, october 6, five Russian climbers were recorded to be dead.

## Why Descents Kill More Climbers Than Summits

While climbs are always difficult and strenuous during summit pushes, most people think it is the key moment that takes a climber's life. But the reality is that most deaths occur during descent rather than the summit push. Some of the key reasons for descents being deadlier than ascents include the following:

*   Physical and mental exhaustion after summit push

*   Running oxygen supplies

*   Rapid drop of temperature and weather changes as day passes

*   Increased risk of frost bites, dehydration, and altitude sickness

*   Simple or minor mistake leading to fall or severe injury

#### Conclusion

Mountains are beautiful land formations touching the high sky and standing in wonder. While they are attractive to visitors and climbers, they also show no mercy to climbers. Mountains like Annapurna I, K2, Kanchenjunga, Dhaulagiri, and Nanga Parbat have shown their brutal side by claiming the life of many brave climbers.

While improved gears, techniques, and technologies have decreased the fatality rate, no one can yet get rid of the challenge that nature brings. The steep ascent, technical difficulties, extreme climate, cold, and low oxygen at the summit are major reasons for deaths in these mountains.

Therefore, bravery along with proper and adequate preparation is a must for increasing the chance of success when sumitting these deadly peaks. Visit [Namas Adventure](https://www.namasadventure.com/) for a successful and safe mountaineering adventure to make your summit dreams come alive.

## FAQs: Deadliest Mountains in the World

### Which is the deadliest mountain in the world?

Annapurna I is considered the deadliest mountain in the world, followed by mountains like Nanga Parbat, K2, Dhaulagiri, and Kanchenjunga. The extreme technical difficulty, risk of avalanche, extreme weather, and lack of oxygen in Annapurna I and other mountains make them the deadliest.

### Is K2 more dangerous than Everest?

Yes, K2 is considered more dangerous than Mount Everest. Although Mount Everest is the highest mountain in the world, K2 has a higher fatality rate of 4:1 deaths on every summit prior to 2021. The technical difficulty, constant falling rocks, harsh weather conditions, steep terrain, and remote location make K2 more dangerous than Everest.

### Why is Nanga Parbat called the Killer Mountain?

Nanga Parbat is also called the **Killer Mountain** due to its fatality rate that claims the life of 1 climber among 5 in each summit attempt. The fatality rate is high, with a 20% to 22% death rate due to steep faces, frequent rock falls, extreme weather, avalanches, and being prone to accidents.

### Mount Everest

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Mount Everest")]

Main article: [List of people who died climbing Mount Everest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_people_who_died_climbing_Mount_Everest "List of people who died climbing Mount Everest")

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/Mount_Everest_North_Face.jpg/250px-Mount_Everest_North_Face.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mount_Everest_North_Face.jpg)

North face of Mount Everest.

[Mount Everest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Everest "Mount Everest"), [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth")'s highest mountain at 8,848.86 metres (29,031.7 ft) above [sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_level "Sea level"), has been host to numerous tragedies. Deaths have occurred on the mountain every year since 1978, excluding 2020, when permits were not issued due to the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronavirus_pandemic "Coronavirus pandemic"). The most notable deadly events on Everest were the [1922 British Mount Everest expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1922_British_Mount_Everest_expedition "1922 British Mount Everest expedition"), [1970 Mount Everest disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1970_Mount_Everest_disaster "1970 Mount Everest disaster"), [1974 French Mount Everest expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_French_Mount_Everest_expedition "1974 French Mount Everest expedition"), [1996 Mount Everest disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_Mount_Everest_disaster "1996 Mount Everest disaster"), [2014 Mount Everest ice avalanche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Mount_Everest_ice_avalanche "2014 Mount Everest ice avalanche"), [2015 Mount Everest avalanches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Mount_Everest_avalanches "2015 Mount Everest avalanches") and [2023 Mount Everest season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_people_who_died_climbing_Mount_Everest#Background "List of people who died climbing Mount Everest"). As of December 2024, there had been 12,884 successful summits, and 340 people had died either before or after reaching the peak.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders#cite_note-www.himalayandatabase.com-1) Since 2019 the Nepali government has initiated periodic "clean-up" campaigns on the mountain, including bodies of climbers.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders#cite_note-2)

### K2

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: K2")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d0/K2_from_North.jpg/250px-K2_from_North.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:K2_from_North.jpg)

Northern vantage of K2.

[K2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K2 "K2") is the world's second-highest mountain at 8,611 meters (28,251 ft) above [sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_level "Sea level"). It lies in the [Karakoram range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karakoram "Karakoram"), partially in the [Gilgit-Baltistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilgit-Baltistan "Gilgit-Baltistan") region of [Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan "Pakistan")-administered [Kashmir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kashmir "Kashmir") and partially in the [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China")-administered [Trans-Karakoram Tract](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trans-Karakoram_Tract "Trans-Karakoram Tract") in the [Taxkorgan Tajik Autonomous County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxkorgan_Tajik_Autonomous_County "Taxkorgan Tajik Autonomous County") of [Xinjiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinjiang "Xinjiang"). While its summit is at a lower altitude than the summit of Mount Everest, it is considered a much harder mountain to climb due to its steep faces and extreme weather. The most deadly events on K2 were the [1986 K2 disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1986_K2_disaster "1986 K2 disaster"), [1995 K2 disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_K2_disaster "1995 K2 disaster"), and [2008 K2 disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_K2_disaster "2008 K2 disaster"). As of August 2023, an estimated 800 people had completed a summit, and 96 had died on the mountain.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders#cite_note-3)

### Kangchenjunga

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Kangchenjunga")]

[![Image 83](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/33/Kangchenjunga.JPG/250px-Kangchenjunga.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kangchenjunga.JPG)

The summit of Kangchenjunga in the background.

[Kangchenjunga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kangchenjunga "Kangchenjunga") is the third-highest mountain in the world. Its summit sits at 8,586 meters (28,169 ft) in a section of the Himalayas called the Kangchenjunga Himal. Because of its remote location in Nepal and the difficulty of accessing it from India, the Kangchenjunga region is not much explored by trekkers. Despite modern improvements to climbing gear, the fatality rate of summit attempts on Kanchenjunga is high. While there had been 532 successful summits as of May 2022, 52 climbers had lost their lives on the mountain. 10 more climbers had died on Yalung Kang (Kangchenjunga West), one of several satellite peaks in the [massif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massif "Massif"), which features routes to the summit of Kangchenjunga.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders#cite_note-www.himalayandatabase.com-1)

### Lhotse

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Lhotse")]

[![Image 125](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/72/Lhotse-fromChukhungRi.jpg/250px-Lhotse-fromChukhungRi.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lhotse-fromChukhungRi.jpg)

The south face of Lhotse, as seen from Chukhung Ri.

Standing at 8,516 meters (27,940 ft) above [sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_level "Sea level"), [Lhotse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lhotse "Lhotse") is the fourth-highest mountain in the world. It is part of the Everest [massif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massif "Massif"), and its standard climbing route follows the same path as Everest's [South Col](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Col "South Col") route up to the [Yellow Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Everest#Geology "Mount Everest") beyond Camp 3. After the Yellow Band, the routes diverge with climbers bound for Everest taking a left over the [Geneva Spur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geneva_Spur "Geneva Spur") up to the South Col, while Lhotse climbers take a right further up the Lhotse face. As of May 2022, there had been 1,089 successful summits and 22 deaths on Lhotse. A further 10 deaths had occurred on [Lhotse Shar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lhotse_Shar "Lhotse Shar"), a subsidiary mountain of Lhotse that offers a more difficult climb to Lhotse's peak than the standard route.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders#cite_note-www.himalayandatabase.com-1)

### Makalu

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Makalu")]

[![Image 155](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Makalu.jpg/250px-Makalu.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Makalu.jpg)

South-western vantage of the Makalu summit.

[Makalu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Makalu "Makalu") is the world's fifth-highest mountain at 8,481 meters (27,825 ft) above [sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_level "Sea level"). It is located in the [Mahalangur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahalangur_Himal "Mahalangur Himal")[Himalayas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himalayas "Himalayas") 19 kilometers (12 mi) southeast of [Mount Everest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Everest "Mount Everest") on the [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China")–[Nepal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepal "Nepal") border. As of December 2024, there had been 800 successful summits of Makalu and 50 deaths on the mountain.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders#cite_note-www.himalayandatabase.com-1)

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/53/Flight_over_himalaya_annotated.jpg/250px-Flight_over_himalaya_annotated.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Flight_over_himalaya_annotated.jpg)

Six of the fourteen summits of the Eight-Thousanders (Manaslu, Shishapangma, Cho Oyu, Lhotse, Mt. Everest and Makalu).

The [eight-thousanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eight-thousander "Eight-thousander") are the 14 [mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain "Mountain") that rise more than 8,000 metres (26,247 ft) above [sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_level "Sea level"). They are all in the [Himalayan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himalayas "Himalayas") and [Karakoram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karakoram "Karakoram")[mountain ranges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain_range "Mountain range"). This is a list of [mountaineers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountaineering "Mountaineering") who have died on these mountains.

### Mount Everest

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Mount Everest")]

Main article: [List of people who died climbing Mount Everest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_people_who_died_climbing_Mount_Everest "List of people who died climbing Mount Everest")

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/Mount_Everest_North_Face.jpg/250px-Mount_Everest_North_Face.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mount_Everest_North_Face.jpg)

North face of Mount Everest.

[Mount Everest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Everest "Mount Everest"), [Earth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth "Earth")'s highest mountain at 8,848.86 metres (29,031.7 ft) above [sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_level "Sea level"), has been host to numerous tragedies. Deaths have occurred on the mountain every year since 1978, excluding 2020, when permits were not issued due to the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronavirus_pandemic "Coronavirus pandemic"). The most notable deadly events on Everest were the [1922 British Mount Everest expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1922_British_Mount_Everest_expedition "1922 British Mount Everest expedition"), [1970 Mount Everest disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1970_Mount_Everest_disaster "1970 Mount Everest disaster"), [1974 French Mount Everest expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_French_Mount_Everest_expedition "1974 French Mount Everest expedition"), [1996 Mount Everest disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_Mount_Everest_disaster "1996 Mount Everest disaster"), [2014 Mount Everest ice avalanche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Mount_Everest_ice_avalanche "2014 Mount Everest ice avalanche"), [2015 Mount Everest avalanches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Mount_Everest_avalanches "2015 Mount Everest avalanches") and [2023 Mount Everest season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_people_who_died_climbing_Mount_Everest#Background "List of people who died climbing Mount Everest"). As of December 2024, there had been 12,884 successful summits, and 340 people had died either before or after reaching the peak.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders#cite_note-www.himalayandatabase.com-1) Since 2019 the Nepali government has initiated periodic "clean-up" campaigns on the mountain, including bodies of climbers.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders#cite_note-2)

### K2

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: K2")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d0/K2_from_North.jpg/250px-K2_from_North.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:K2_from_North.jpg)

Northern vantage of K2.

[K2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K2 "K2") is the world's second-highest mountain at 8,611 meters (28,251 ft) above [sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_level "Sea level"). It lies in the [Karakoram range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karakoram "Karakoram"), partially in the [Gilgit-Baltistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilgit-Baltistan "Gilgit-Baltistan") region of [Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan "Pakistan")-administered [Kashmir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kashmir "Kashmir") and partially in the [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China")-administered [Trans-Karakoram Tract](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trans-Karakoram_Tract "Trans-Karakoram Tract") in the [Taxkorgan Tajik Autonomous County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taxkorgan_Tajik_Autonomous_County "Taxkorgan Tajik Autonomous County") of [Xinjiang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xinjiang "Xinjiang"). While its summit is at a lower altitude than the summit of Mount Everest, it is considered a much harder mountain to climb due to its steep faces and extreme weather. The most deadly events on K2 were the [1986 K2 disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1986_K2_disaster "1986 K2 disaster"), [1995 K2 disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_K2_disaster "1995 K2 disaster"), and [2008 K2 disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_K2_disaster "2008 K2 disaster"). As of August 2023, an estimated 800 people had completed a summit, and 96 had died on the mountain.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders#cite_note-3)

### Kangchenjunga

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Kangchenjunga")]

[![Image 83](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/33/Kangchenjunga.JPG/250px-Kangchenjunga.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kangchenjunga.JPG)

The summit of Kangchenjunga in the background.

[Kangchenjunga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kangchenjunga "Kangchenjunga") is the third-highest mountain in the world. Its summit sits at 8,586 meters (28,169 ft) in a section of the Himalayas called the Kangchenjunga Himal. Because of its remote location in Nepal and the difficulty of accessing it from India, the Kangchenjunga region is not much explored by trekkers. Despite modern improvements to climbing gear, the fatality rate of summit attempts on Kanchenjunga is high. While there had been 532 successful summits as of May 2022, 52 climbers had lost their lives on the mountain. 10 more climbers had died on Yalung Kang (Kangchenjunga West), one of several satellite peaks in the [massif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massif "Massif"), which features routes to the summit of Kangchenjunga.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders#cite_note-www.himalayandatabase.com-1)

### Lhotse

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Lhotse")]

[![Image 125](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/72/Lhotse-fromChukhungRi.jpg/250px-Lhotse-fromChukhungRi.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lhotse-fromChukhungRi.jpg)

The south face of Lhotse, as seen from Chukhung Ri.

Standing at 8,516 meters (27,940 ft) above [sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_level "Sea level"), [Lhotse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lhotse "Lhotse") is the fourth-highest mountain in the world. It is part of the Everest [massif](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massif "Massif"), and its standard climbing route follows the same path as Everest's [South Col](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Col "South Col") route up to the [Yellow Band](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Everest#Geology "Mount Everest") beyond Camp 3. After the Yellow Band, the routes diverge with climbers bound for Everest taking a left over the [Geneva Spur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geneva_Spur "Geneva Spur") up to the South Col, while Lhotse climbers take a right further up the Lhotse face. As of May 2022, there had been 1,089 successful summits and 22 deaths on Lhotse. A further 10 deaths had occurred on [Lhotse Shar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lhotse_Shar "Lhotse Shar"), a subsidiary mountain of Lhotse that offers a more difficult climb to Lhotse's peak than the standard route.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders#cite_note-www.himalayandatabase.com-1)

### Makalu

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Makalu")]

[![Image 155](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/19/Makalu.jpg/250px-Makalu.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Makalu.jpg)

South-western vantage of the Makalu summit.

[Makalu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Makalu "Makalu") is the world's fifth-highest mountain at 8,481 meters (27,825 ft) above [sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_level "Sea level"). It is located in the [Mahalangur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahalangur_Himal "Mahalangur Himal")[Himalayas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himalayas "Himalayas") 19 kilometers (12 mi) southeast of [Mount Everest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Everest "Mount Everest") on the [China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China")–[Nepal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepal "Nepal") border. As of December 2024, there had been 800 successful summits of Makalu and 50 deaths on the mountain.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_deaths_on_eight-thousanders#cite_note-www.himalayandatabase.com-1)

### THE HISTORY OF H.P. HERCULES

## RELIABLE AND ROBUST LUXURY WATCHES MADE BY HENZI & PFAFF

Learn how Hercules conveyed luxury into strength and resistance by putting their watch to the ultimate test.

#### EXPLORE NOW

### MADE IN SWITZERLAND

Hercules offers two high-quality Swiss-made mechanical movement options for their watches, each with its own unique features and advantages:

**Micro Rotor Movement**: This movement is designed with a micro rotor, which is asmall automatic winding system that helps power the watch. One key benefit of this design is that it allows for a thinner overall watch profile compared to regular automatic watches that rely on the movement of your wrist to wind. Additionally,the placement of the micro rotor allows for a close fit between the movement and the anti-reflective coated sapphire caseback,giving the wearer a clear view of the intricate mechanics of the watch and the decorated bridges with Superluminova-filled height lines.

**Hand Wound Movement with Two Barrels**: The hand-wound movement with two barrels provides an impressive 120 hours (5days) of power reserve. Hand-wound movements are appreciated by watch enthusiasts for their simplicity and the connection they offer to the watch’s inner workings. Through the caseback, you can get an up-close view of the movement,including engraved height lines representing the Nanga Parbat mountain, which are filled with Swiss BGW9 SuperLuminova for a striking glow in the dark.

Furthermore, each Hercules watch is assembled by hand, emphasizing the craftsmanship andattention to detail that goes into its production. To ensure accuracy and precision, the complete watch undergoes testing by [Timelab](https://www.timelab.ch/) inSwitzerland to receive an official “Observatoire Chronométrique+” certification. If the watch successfully passes this test,it earns the prestigious title of a “Chronometer,” signifying its exceptional timekeeping performance.

### NANGA PARBAT, one of the few +8’000m peaks in the world

In 1953, an Austrian mountaineer called Hermann Buhl became the first one to reach the top of the Nanga Parbat (8’126M). 31 Men tried to do this before him but didn’t return, which gave the Nanga Parbat the nickname “Killer Mountain”. Hermann and the entire expedition crew were equipped with Hercules timepieces made by the watchmaking atelier Henzi & Pfaff. The watches proved to be reliable, robust, and precise timekeepers during their adventure.After none of the experimental clocks failed, Henzi & Pfaff successfully placed the proven reliability under extreme weather conditions at the center of its advertising. This was reinforced by the presence of the distinctive brand Hercules, which conveyed strength and resistance. The successful ascent and the worldwide attention of the expedition were marketed effectively by Henzi & Pfaff. As a result, Henzi & Pfaff equipped further expeditions with watches and thus developed the image of a reliable, robust and at the same time sporty watch.

## the most complete and advanced mountaineer of his time

### HERMANN **BUHL**

(21 September 1924 – 27 June 1957) Hermann was an Austrian mountaineer and is considered one of the best climbers of all time. He was particularly innovative in applying Alpine style climbing to Himalayan climbing.

![Image 4: nanga-parbat-mountain-top2](https://herculeswatches.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/nanga-parbat-mountain-top2.jpg)

#### First ascent

1953 First ascent of Nanga Parbat, 8126 m (26,660 ft) (solo and without bottled oxygen). On the way back from the summit he was forced to stand erect on a rock ledge for the entire night at 8000 m altitude, in order to survive until the following morning.

#### First to succeed

Before his successful Nanga Parbat expedition, 31 people had died trying to make the first ascent.

#### Solo mountaineer

Buhl is the only mountaineer to have made the first ascent of an eight-thousander solo. His climbing partner, Otto Kempter, was too slow in joining the ascent, so Buhl struck off alone. He returned 41 hours later, having barely survived the arduous climb to the summit, 6.5 km (4 miles) distant from, and 1.2 km (4,000 feet) higher then, camp V.

#### Alpine style mountaineering

Buhl can be considered a pioneer of Alpine style mountaineering in the Himalayas, a style defined by light-weight expedition gear, little to no fixed ropes and the relinquishing of bottled oxygen.

### THE BOOK: NANGA PARBAT PILGRIMAGE

There is also a book written about the adventure of Hermann Buhl climbing the mountain.  
 In 1953 Hermann Buhl made the first ascent of Nanga Parbat – the ninth-highest mountain in the world, and the third 8,000-metre peak to be climbed, following Annapurna and Everest. It was one of the most incredible and committed climbs ever made. Continuing alone and without supplementary oxygen, Buhl made a dash for the summit after his partners turned back. On a mountain that had claimed thirty-one lives, an exhausted Buhl waded through deep snow and climbed over technical ground to reach the summit, driven on by an ‘irresistible urge’. After a night spent standing on a small ledge at over 8,000 metres, Buhl returned forty-one hours later, exhausted and at the very limit of his endurance.Written shortly after Buhl’s return from the mountain, Nanga Parbat Pilgrimage is a classic of mountaineering literature that has inspired thousands of climbers. It follows Buhl’s inexorable rise from rock climber to alpinist to mountaineer, until, almost inevitably, he makes his phenomenal Nanga Parbat climb. Buhl’s book, and ascent, reminded everyone that, while the mountains could never be conquered, they could be climbed with sufficient enthusiasm, spirit and dedication.

#### MOVIES

### On the big screen

The Climb is a Canadian-British coproduced adventure drama film directed by Donald Shebib and released in 1986. A dramatization of mountaineer Hermann Buhl’s 1953 attempt to climb Nanga Parbat, the film stars Bruce Greenwood as Buhl alongside James Hurdle, Kenneth Welsh, Ken Pogue, Thomas Hauff, Guy Bannerman, David James Elliott, and Tom Butler as members of his expedition

The film was broadcast on British television in 1986 as part of Mountain Men, a series of three films dramatizing noteworthy historical climbing expeditions. In Canada, it was announced in the Perspectives Canada program at both the 1986 Toronto International Film Festival[3] and the 1987 Toronto International Film Festival.

The film received two Genie Award nominations at the 9th Genie Awards in 1988, for Best Cinematography (Richard Leiterman) and Best Sound Editing (Robin Leigh, Richard Cadger, Jane Tattersall, Penny Hozy, and Peter McBurnie). Leiterman received the Canadian Society of Cinematographers Feature Award for his film in 1988.

### Nanga Parbat 1953

This movie is a documentary directed by Hans Ertl (1908–2000). He was a mountaineer and was considered one of the best cameramen of his time. He specialized in mountain, sports, and expedition films. In this role, he accompanied the expedition to Nanga Parbat.

He was part of the expedition on the mountain, so all the footage is real-life footage from the climb, making it even more precise. The coolest thing is that you can see the expedition members wearing the Hercules Watches! The movie was broadcasted on German national television on the 17th of June 1969. At that time, the Henzi & Pfaff factory was still active and producing their watches.

### THE HISTORY OF H.P. HERCULES

## RELIABLE AND ROBUST LUXURY WATCHES MADE BY HENZI & PFAFF

Learn how Hercules conveyed luxury into strength and resistance by putting their watch to the ultimate test.

#### EXPLORE NOW

### MADE IN SWITZERLAND

Hercules offers two high-quality Swiss-made mechanical movement options for their watches, each with its own unique features and advantages:

**Micro Rotor Movement**: This movement is designed with a micro rotor, which is asmall automatic winding system that helps power the watch. One key benefit of this design is that it allows for a thinner overall watch profile compared to regular automatic watches that rely on the movement of your wrist to wind. Additionally,the placement of the micro rotor allows for a close fit between the movement and the anti-reflective coated sapphire caseback,giving the wearer a clear view of the intricate mechanics of the watch and the decorated bridges with Superluminova-filled height lines.

**Hand Wound Movement with Two Barrels**: The hand-wound movement with two barrels provides an impressive 120 hours (5days) of power reserve. Hand-wound movements are appreciated by watch enthusiasts for their simplicity and the connection they offer to the watch’s inner workings. Through the caseback, you can get an up-close view of the movement,including engraved height lines representing the Nanga Parbat mountain, which are filled with Swiss BGW9 SuperLuminova for a striking glow in the dark.

Furthermore, each Hercules watch is assembled by hand, emphasizing the craftsmanship andattention to detail that goes into its production. To ensure accuracy and precision, the complete watch undergoes testing by [Timelab](https://www.timelab.ch/) inSwitzerland to receive an official “Observatoire Chronométrique+” certification. If the watch successfully passes this test,it earns the prestigious title of a “Chronometer,” signifying its exceptional timekeeping performance.

### NANGA PARBAT, one of the few +8’000m peaks in the world

In 1953, an Austrian mountaineer called Hermann Buhl became the first one to reach the top of the Nanga Parbat (8’126M). 31 Men tried to do this before him but didn’t return, which gave the Nanga Parbat the nickname “Killer Mountain”. Hermann and the entire expedition crew were equipped with Hercules timepieces made by the watchmaking atelier Henzi & Pfaff. The watches proved to be reliable, robust, and precise timekeepers during their adventure.After none of the experimental clocks failed, Henzi & Pfaff successfully placed the proven reliability under extreme weather conditions at the center of its advertising. This was reinforced by the presence of the distinctive brand Hercules, which conveyed strength and resistance. The successful ascent and the worldwide attention of the expedition were marketed effectively by Henzi & Pfaff. As a result, Henzi & Pfaff equipped further expeditions with watches and thus developed the image of a reliable, robust and at the same time sporty watch.

## the most complete and advanced mountaineer of his time

### HERMANN **BUHL**

(21 September 1924 – 27 June 1957) Hermann was an Austrian mountaineer and is considered one of the best climbers of all time. He was particularly innovative in applying Alpine style climbing to Himalayan climbing.

![Image 4: nanga-parbat-mountain-top2](https://herculeswatches.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/nanga-parbat-mountain-top2.jpg)

#### First ascent

1953 First ascent of Nanga Parbat, 8126 m (26,660 ft) (solo and without bottled oxygen). On the way back from the summit he was forced to stand erect on a rock ledge for the entire night at 8000 m altitude, in order to survive until the following morning.

#### First to succeed

Before his successful Nanga Parbat expedition, 31 people had died trying to make the first ascent.

#### Solo mountaineer

Buhl is the only mountaineer to have made the first ascent of an eight-thousander solo. His climbing partner, Otto Kempter, was too slow in joining the ascent, so Buhl struck off alone. He returned 41 hours later, having barely survived the arduous climb to the summit, 6.5 km (4 miles) distant from, and 1.2 km (4,000 feet) higher then, camp V.

#### Alpine style mountaineering

Buhl can be considered a pioneer of Alpine style mountaineering in the Himalayas, a style defined by light-weight expedition gear, little to no fixed ropes and the relinquishing of bottled oxygen.

### THE BOOK: NANGA PARBAT PILGRIMAGE

There is also a book written about the adventure of Hermann Buhl climbing the mountain.  
 In 1953 Hermann Buhl made the first ascent of Nanga Parbat – the ninth-highest mountain in the world, and the third 8,000-metre peak to be climbed, following Annapurna and Everest. It was one of the most incredible and committed climbs ever made. Continuing alone and without supplementary oxygen, Buhl made a dash for the summit after his partners turned back. On a mountain that had claimed thirty-one lives, an exhausted Buhl waded through deep snow and climbed over technical ground to reach the summit, driven on by an ‘irresistible urge’. After a night spent standing on a small ledge at over 8,000 metres, Buhl returned forty-one hours later, exhausted and at the very limit of his endurance.Written shortly after Buhl’s return from the mountain, Nanga Parbat Pilgrimage is a classic of mountaineering literature that has inspired thousands of climbers. It follows Buhl’s inexorable rise from rock climber to alpinist to mountaineer, until, almost inevitably, he makes his phenomenal Nanga Parbat climb. Buhl’s book, and ascent, reminded everyone that, while the mountains could never be conquered, they could be climbed with sufficient enthusiasm, spirit and dedication.

#### MOVIES

### On the big screen

The Climb is a Canadian-British coproduced adventure drama film directed by Donald Shebib and released in 1986. A dramatization of mountaineer Hermann Buhl’s 1953 attempt to climb Nanga Parbat, the film stars Bruce Greenwood as Buhl alongside James Hurdle, Kenneth Welsh, Ken Pogue, Thomas Hauff, Guy Bannerman, David James Elliott, and Tom Butler as members of his expedition

The film was broadcast on British television in 1986 as part of Mountain Men, a series of three films dramatizing noteworthy historical climbing expeditions. In Canada, it was announced in the Perspectives Canada program at both the 1986 Toronto International Film Festival[3] and the 1987 Toronto International Film Festival.

The film received two Genie Award nominations at the 9th Genie Awards in 1988, for Best Cinematography (Richard Leiterman) and Best Sound Editing (Robin Leigh, Richard Cadger, Jane Tattersall, Penny Hozy, and Peter McBurnie). Leiterman received the Canadian Society of Cinematographers Feature Award for his film in 1988.

# Hercules

![Image 2](https://www.swiss-pavilion.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/hercules_logo-300x188.png)

### Hercules

In 1953, Hermann Buhl, an Austrian mountaineer, achieved the historic feat of being the first person to scale the 8,126-meter Nanga Parbat mountain. Wearing a Hercules watch around his wrist, this triumph marked a pivotal moment in the history of mountaineering. In the years before, watchmaker Robert Pfaff, hailing from a family with a legacy of watch manufacturing in Pforzheim during the 1920s and 1930s, joined forces with Robert Henzi around 1946 to establish a new company.  
 By 1952, Henzi & Pfaff had grown to employ over 200 individuals, opening a manufacturing facility in Stein, Germany. Their strategic marketing efforts reached new heights in 1953 when they provided their Hercules timepieces to the German-Austrian mountaineering group attempting the first ascent of Nanga Parbat. The success of the expedition, coupled with Henzi & Pfaff’s effective marketing, solidified the brand’s reputation for producing reliable, robust, and sporty watches.

In the iconic ascent, Buhl set out from the base camp at 02:00 on July 3, 1953, and by 19:00, he stood alone at the summit, becoming the first person to conquer an 8,000-meter peak solo. Unable to return to the base camp, Buhl spent a challenging night on a small ledge with minimal space. Eventually, he reached one of the base camps the following day, surprising expedition members who had assumed he perished. Buhl’s remarkable achievements made him a legendary figure, inspiring numerous books and two movies.

Today, the brand has reintroduced an exclusive series of watches inspired by the original timepieces that accompanied Buhl on his historic ascent. The micro-rotor movement, developed over three years, is tailor-made for Hercules watches. Last year the hand wound movement with 120 hours power reserve was added. Each movement undergoes rigorous testing by the Timelab institute in Geneva,Switzerland, accompanied by an official certificate. The movement’s bridges feature engraved height lines of the Nanga Parbat mountain, and the rotor’s logo is filled with BRW9 SuperLuminova, illuminating in bright blue reminiscent of the permafrost ice atop the mountain, creating a captivating and magical effect.

# Hercules

![Image 2](https://www.swiss-pavilion.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/03/hercules_logo-300x188.png)

### Hercules

In 1953, Hermann Buhl, an Austrian mountaineer, achieved the historic feat of being the first person to scale the 8,126-meter Nanga Parbat mountain. Wearing a Hercules watch around his wrist, this triumph marked a pivotal moment in the history of mountaineering. In the years before, watchmaker Robert Pfaff, hailing from a family with a legacy of watch manufacturing in Pforzheim during the 1920s and 1930s, joined forces with Robert Henzi around 1946 to establish a new company.  
 By 1952, Henzi & Pfaff had grown to employ over 200 individuals, opening a manufacturing facility in Stein, Germany. Their strategic marketing efforts reached new heights in 1953 when they provided their Hercules timepieces to the German-Austrian mountaineering group attempting the first ascent of Nanga Parbat. The success of the expedition, coupled with Henzi & Pfaff’s effective marketing, solidified the brand’s reputation for producing reliable, robust, and sporty watches.

In the iconic ascent, Buhl set out from the base camp at 02:00 on July 3, 1953, and by 19:00, he stood alone at the summit, becoming the first person to conquer an 8,000-meter peak solo. Unable to return to the base camp, Buhl spent a challenging night on a small ledge with minimal space. Eventually, he reached one of the base camps the following day, surprising expedition members who had assumed he perished. Buhl’s remarkable achievements made him a legendary figure, inspiring numerous books and two movies.

Today, the brand has reintroduced an exclusive series of watches inspired by the original timepieces that accompanied Buhl on his historic ascent. The micro-rotor movement, developed over three years, is tailor-made for Hercules watches. Last year the hand wound movement with 120 hours power reserve was added. Each movement undergoes rigorous testing by the Timelab institute in Geneva,Switzerland, accompanied by an official certificate. The movement’s bridges feature engraved height lines of the Nanga Parbat mountain, and the rotor’s logo is filled with BRW9 SuperLuminova, illuminating in bright blue reminiscent of the permafrost ice atop the mountain, creating a captivating and magical effect.

**Hermann Buhl** (21 September 1924[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-Messner-1) – 27 June 1957) was an Austrian [mountaineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountaineering "Mountaineering"). His accomplishments include the first ascents of [Nanga Parbat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanga_Parbat "Nanga Parbat") in 1953 and [Broad Peak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broad_Peak "Broad Peak") in 1957. He was one of the pioneers of the [alpine style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpine_style "Alpine style"). Buhl was the father of Austrian–German writer, publisher, and [freelance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freelance "Freelance") journalist, Kriemhild "Krimi" Buhl.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-2)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hermann_Buhl&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Buhl was born in [Innsbruck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Innsbruck "Innsbruck"), [Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Austrian_Republic "First Austrian Republic"). He was the youngest of four children. At the age of four, he was taken to an orphanage with his half-brother Siegfried after his mother Marianne, who came from [South Tyrol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Tyrol "South Tyrol"), became mentally ill and was institutionalized.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-Messner-1) His father Wilhelm, unable to cope with raising four children alone, told them their mother had died. However, Marianne was later murdered by the [Nazis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Germany "Nazi Germany") at [Mauthausen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mauthausen_concentration_camp "Mauthausen concentration camp").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-3) He was later taken in by his aunt and uncle.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-4) In the 1930s, considered a weak and sensitive boy, he made his first climbing trips in the [Tux Alps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tux_Alps "Tux Alps"), the [Wilder Kaiser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilder_Kaiser "Wilder Kaiser"), and the [Karwendel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karwendel "Karwendel"). In 1939, he joined the youth group of the Innsbruck section, which belonged to the [German Alpine Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Alpine_Club "German Alpine Club") (DAV) from 1938 to 1945. Later, together with his friend [Kurt Diemberger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurt_Diemberger "Kurt Diemberger"), he was a member of the Bergland section of the DAV in [Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich "Munich"). With [Luis Trenker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luis_Trenker "Luis Trenker")'s help, the section's founder, [August Schuster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/August_Schuster?action=edit&redlink=1 "August Schuster (page does not exist)"), gave him a job in his sports shop.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-5)

After finishing secondary school, Buhl began an apprenticeship as a forwarding agent. [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") interrupted his commercial training, and in 1943 he joined the [Alpine troops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpine_troops "Alpine troops") as a mountain infantryman. Buhl participated in the [Battle of Monte Cassino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Monte_Cassino "Battle of Monte Cassino") in [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Italy "Kingdom of Italy").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-Evil_Style_Queen-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-7) In 1949 he was a founding member of the Innsbruck [mountain rescue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain_rescue "Mountain rescue") group.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-8)

In March 1951, Buhl married Eugenie ("Generl") Högerle (died 2025) from [Ramsau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramsau_bei_Berchtesgaden "Ramsau bei Berchtesgaden") near [Berchtesgaden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berchtesgaden "Berchtesgaden") and in the same year became the father of Kriemhild Buhl, who would later become a writer. Two more daughters, Silvia[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-9) and Ingrid, who died young,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-10) followed, and the family moved to his wife's hometown.

In 1957, Hermann Buhl was photographed with his wife and daughter in [Vienna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna "Vienna") before departing for the [Broad Peak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broad_Peak "Broad Peak") expedition.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-11)[_[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable\_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_] Less is known about Buhl's other daughters. In her book _Papa Lalalaya_, Kriemhild Buhl recounts her father's fame after the Nanga Parbat ascent and its effect on the family; she and her two younger sisters saw little of their father in his later years, as his mountaineering career and public engagements frequently kept him away from home.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-12)

As a [mountain guide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain_guide "Mountain guide") he earned little, so to support his family he also worked as a [salesman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sales "Sales") and equipment advisor at Sporthaus Schuster, a sportswear store in [Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich "Munich").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-Evil_Style_Queen-6)

## Alpinism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hermann_Buhl&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Alpinism")]

### Nanga Parbat

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hermann_Buhl&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Nanga Parbat")]

Main article: [1953 German–Austrian Nanga Parbat expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1953_German%E2%80%93Austrian_Nanga_Parbat_expedition "1953 German–Austrian Nanga Parbat expedition")

Before his successful 1953 [Nanga Parbat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanga_Parbat "Nanga Parbat") expedition, 31 people had died trying to make the first ascent.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-Buhllaw-13)

The ascent of Nanga Parbat on 3 July 1953 is Buhl's best-known achievement. It took place as part of the _[Willy Merkl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willy\_Merkl "Willy Merkl") Memorial Expedition_, organized and led by the Munich doctor [Karl Herrligkoffer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Herrligkoffer "Karl Herrligkoffer"), with [Peter Aschenbrenner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Aschenbrenner?action=edit&redlink=1 "Peter Aschenbrenner (page does not exist)") serving as alpine adviser.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-AJ-buhl-14) A change in the weather after an initial monsoon helped Buhl's group. On 2 July they reached Camp V at 6,900 m (22,638 ft): Buhl, Walter Frauenberger,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-15)[Hans Ertl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Ertl_(cameraman) "Hans Ertl (cameraman)"), and Otto Kempter. Buhl and Kempter spent the night there, while the other two descended with the porters to Camp IV.

Buhl set off for the summit alone and without additional oxygen at around 02:30, finally reaching it with his last reserves of strength at around 19:00. As proof of his ascent, he left his ice axe and the [Pakistani flag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flag_of_Pakistan "Flag of Pakistan") at the summit. Kempter, who had set off an hour later, was forced to turn back after a bout of weakness at an altitude of around 7,400 m (24,278 ft) on the plateau at the Silbersattel. He returned to Camp V, where he waited with Frauenberger and Ertl, who had climbed back up, for Buhl to return.

Buhl spent the following night alone, about 1.2 km (4,000 feet) higher up than Camp V. He survived the night at an altitude of almost 8,000 m (26,200 ft) without bivouac equipment only because of unusually favourable weather.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-AJ-buhl-14) However, he suffered [frostbite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frostbite "Frostbite") on two of his toes and still had most of the descent ahead of him. At times he fell into a dangerous state of apathy and suffered perceptual illusions, which he combated with [Pervitin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pervitin "Pervitin").

After 41 hours and in states of extreme exhaustion and dehydration, Buhl arrived back at Camp V, where hopes of his return had already begun to fade.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-AJ-buhl-14) In the days that followed, he also completed the descent to the main camp unaided, arriving there on 7 July. Here it turned out that the big toe and part of the second toe on his right foot could not be saved and had to be amputated.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-16) He therefore had to be carried on the rest of the return march.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Hans Ertl made a documentary film called _Nanga Parbat_ about this expedition.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-17)

A dispute arose between Herrligkoffer and Buhl after the expedition due to Herrligkoffer's authoritarian leadership and Buhl's refusal to follow orders without question. Expedition members had contractually ceded sole exploitation rights over the expedition's results to Herrligkoffer, and his rigorous enforcement of this clause led to a protracted legal dispute with Buhl and Hans Ertl.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-18)

Buhl is the only mountaineer to have made the first ascent of an [eight-thousander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eight-thousander "Eight-thousander") solo, achieved on his first visit to the [Greater Ranges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roof_of_the_World "Roof of the World").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-Isserman-19) His monumental efforts, which included spending the night standing untethered on a tiny pedestal, too small to crouch on, at the edge of a 60-degree ice slope, have become mountaineering legend, described by [Bonington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Bonington "Chris Bonington") as "a magnificent achievement".[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-Quest-20)

In 1999, Buhl's ice axe, which had been left behind on the summit, was found by a Japanese expedition and returned to his widow.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-21)

### Broad Peak

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hermann_Buhl&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Broad Peak")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cc/Buhl_Bergland-Wimpel.jpg/250px-Buhl_Bergland-Wimpel.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Buhl_Bergland-Wimpel.jpg)

Hermann Buhl memorial plaque in the August-Schuster-Haus with original pennant

[Fritz Wintersteller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fritz_Wintersteller "Fritz Wintersteller") and [Kurt Diemberger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurt_Diemberger "Kurt Diemberger") reached the forepeak (8,030 m (26,345 ft)) on 29 May 1957, during the course of the Austrian expedition led by [Marcus Schmuck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Schmuck "Marcus Schmuck"). However, it was a few days later, between 8 and 9 June, that Wintersteller, Schmuck, Diemberger, and Buhl reached the true summit of [Broad Peak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broad_Peak "Broad Peak") (8,051 m (26,414 ft)) and achieved the first successful ascent of the mountain. Buhl approached the summit in the twilight, at around 18:30.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-DiemBroad-22) The ascent was accomplished without the aid of supplemental oxygen, high-altitude porters or base camp support.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-DiemBroad-22) The original pennant bearing the Bergland section's emblem, which appears in Buhl's summit photo, is on display in the restaurant of the [August-Schuster-Haus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/August-Schuster-Haus?action=edit&redlink=1 "August-Schuster-Haus (page does not exist)") in [Garmisch-Partenkirchen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garmisch-Partenkirchen "Garmisch-Partenkirchen"). This summit photo and Buhl's last letter to his comrades from Bergland can be found in the commemorative publication for the 50th anniversary of the Bergland section in 1958.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-23)

### Chogolisa

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hermann_Buhl&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Chogolisa")]

Just a few weeks after the successful [first ascent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_ascent "First ascent") of Broad Peak, Buhl and Diemberger made an attempt on nearby, unclimbed [Chogolisa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chogolisa "Chogolisa") (7,665 m (25,148 ft)) in [Alpine style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpine_style "Alpine style").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-24) Buhl lost his way in an unexpected snowstorm on the southeast ridge, near the summit of Chogolisa II (7,654 m (25,112 ft); also known as Bride Peak), and walked over a huge [cornice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornice_(climbing) "Cornice (climbing)") overhanging the mountain's north face, subsequently triggering an [avalanche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avalanche "Avalanche") that hurled him down the face.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-DiemBroad-22) His body could not be recovered and remains in the ice. After losing sight of Buhl in the storm, Diemberger, who was climbing with him, found his footsteps leading to a fresh breach in the cornice.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-DiemBroad-22)

## Legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hermann_Buhl&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Legacy")]

Buhl was the first person to climb an eight-thousander on the final section alone and without additional oxygen.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-Isserman-19) Austrian sports journalists voted him "[Sportsman of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austrian_Sports_Personality_of_the_Year "Austrian Sports Personality of the Year") 1953" on 21 January 1954.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-25)

Because of his prominent first ascents in the Alps and the [Karakoram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karakoram "Karakoram"), [Reinhold Messner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinhold_Messner "Reinhold Messner") has described Buhl as the best all-round mountaineer of his time.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-26) His solo ascent of Nanga Parbat was made against explicit orders. This sat uneasily with the nationalist framing under which the West German and Austrian public had followed the expedition, since the mountain had been styled as a "German fate-mountain" (_Schicksalsberg der Deutschen_) after earlier German expeditions in the 1930s.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-27) Rather than mounting heavily equipped, large-scale expeditions, he preferred travelling light, climbing fast, and forgoing supplemental oxygen. He was also a role model for climbers of younger generations, including [Reinhold Messner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinhold_Messner "Reinhold Messner")[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-Buhllaw-13) and [Peter Habeler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Habeler "Peter Habeler"), who cited Buhl as one of his inspirations.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-28)

In 2006, the Austrian mountaineer and alpine historian [Markus Kronthaler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markus_Kronthaler "Markus Kronthaler") died from exhaustion during the descent after reaching the summit of Broad Peak.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-29)

### Honoring

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hermann_Buhl&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Honoring")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/58/Hermann-Buhl_Platz_Innsbruck_2023-09-25_01.jpg/250px-Hermann-Buhl_Platz_Innsbruck_2023-09-25_01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hermann-Buhl_Platz_Innsbruck_2023-09-25_01.jpg)

Hermann-Buhl Platz Innsbruck

On 24 September 2012, the previously unnamed square in front of the [Hungerburgbahn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungerburgbahn "Hungerburgbahn") mountain station in Innsbruck was named Hermann-Buhl-Platz after Hermann Buhl.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-31)

His expedition to Nanga Parbat was dramatized by [Donald Shebib](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Shebib "Donald Shebib") in the 1986 film _[The Climb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Climb\_(1986\_film) "The Climb (1986 film)")_, based in part on Buhl's own writings about the expedition and starring [Bruce Greenwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Greenwood "Bruce Greenwood") as Buhl.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-groen-32)
