**Hermann Buhl** (21 September 1924[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-Messner-1) – 27 June 1957) was an Austrian [mountaineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountaineering "Mountaineering"). His accomplishments include the first ascents of [Nanga Parbat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanga_Parbat "Nanga Parbat") in 1953 and [Broad Peak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broad_Peak "Broad Peak") in 1957. He was one of the pioneers of the [alpine style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpine_style "Alpine style"). Buhl was the father of Austrian–German writer, publisher, and [freelance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freelance "Freelance") journalist, Kriemhild "Krimi" Buhl.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-2)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hermann_Buhl&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Buhl was born in [Innsbruck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Innsbruck "Innsbruck"), [Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Austrian_Republic "First Austrian Republic"). He was the youngest of four children. At the age of four, he was taken to an orphanage with his half-brother Siegfried after his mother Marianne, who came from [South Tyrol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Tyrol "South Tyrol"), became mentally ill and was institutionalized.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-Messner-1) His father Wilhelm, unable to cope with raising four children alone, told them their mother had died. However, Marianne was later murdered by the [Nazis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Germany "Nazi Germany") at [Mauthausen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mauthausen_concentration_camp "Mauthausen concentration camp").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-3) He was later taken in by his aunt and uncle.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-4) In the 1930s, considered a weak and sensitive boy, he made his first climbing trips in the [Tux Alps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tux_Alps "Tux Alps"), the [Wilder Kaiser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilder_Kaiser "Wilder Kaiser"), and the [Karwendel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karwendel "Karwendel"). In 1939, he joined the youth group of the Innsbruck section, which belonged to the [German Alpine Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_Alpine_Club "German Alpine Club") (DAV) from 1938 to 1945. Later, together with his friend [Kurt Diemberger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurt_Diemberger "Kurt Diemberger"), he was a member of the Bergland section of the DAV in [Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich "Munich"). With [Luis Trenker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luis_Trenker "Luis Trenker")'s help, the section's founder, [August Schuster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/August_Schuster?action=edit&redlink=1 "August Schuster (page does not exist)"), gave him a job in his sports shop.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-5)

After finishing secondary school, Buhl began an apprenticeship as a forwarding agent. [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") interrupted his commercial training, and in 1943 he joined the [Alpine troops](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpine_troops "Alpine troops") as a mountain infantryman. Buhl participated in the [Battle of Monte Cassino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Monte_Cassino "Battle of Monte Cassino") in [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Italy "Kingdom of Italy").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-Evil_Style_Queen-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-7) In 1949 he was a founding member of the Innsbruck [mountain rescue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain_rescue "Mountain rescue") group.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-8)

In March 1951, Buhl married Eugenie ("Generl") Högerle (died 2025) from [Ramsau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramsau_bei_Berchtesgaden "Ramsau bei Berchtesgaden") near [Berchtesgaden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berchtesgaden "Berchtesgaden") and in the same year became the father of Kriemhild Buhl, who would later become a writer. Two more daughters, Silvia[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-9) and Ingrid, who died young,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-10) followed, and the family moved to his wife's hometown.

In 1957, Hermann Buhl was photographed with his wife and daughter in [Vienna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna "Vienna") before departing for the [Broad Peak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broad_Peak "Broad Peak") expedition.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-11)[_[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable\_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_] Less is known about Buhl's other daughters. In her book _Papa Lalalaya_, Kriemhild Buhl recounts her father's fame after the Nanga Parbat ascent and its effect on the family; she and her two younger sisters saw little of their father in his later years, as his mountaineering career and public engagements frequently kept him away from home.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-12)

As a [mountain guide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain_guide "Mountain guide") he earned little, so to support his family he also worked as a [salesman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sales "Sales") and equipment advisor at Sporthaus Schuster, a sportswear store in [Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich "Munich").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-Evil_Style_Queen-6)

## Alpinism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hermann_Buhl&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Alpinism")]

### Nanga Parbat

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hermann_Buhl&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Nanga Parbat")]

Main article: [1953 German–Austrian Nanga Parbat expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1953_German%E2%80%93Austrian_Nanga_Parbat_expedition "1953 German–Austrian Nanga Parbat expedition")

Before his successful 1953 [Nanga Parbat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nanga_Parbat "Nanga Parbat") expedition, 31 people had died trying to make the first ascent.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-Buhllaw-13)

The ascent of Nanga Parbat on 3 July 1953 is Buhl's best-known achievement. It took place as part of the _[Willy Merkl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willy\_Merkl "Willy Merkl") Memorial Expedition_, organized and led by the Munich doctor [Karl Herrligkoffer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Herrligkoffer "Karl Herrligkoffer"), with [Peter Aschenbrenner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Aschenbrenner?action=edit&redlink=1 "Peter Aschenbrenner (page does not exist)") serving as alpine adviser.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-AJ-buhl-14) A change in the weather after an initial monsoon helped Buhl's group. On 2 July they reached Camp V at 6,900 m (22,638 ft): Buhl, Walter Frauenberger,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-15)[Hans Ertl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Ertl_(cameraman) "Hans Ertl (cameraman)"), and Otto Kempter. Buhl and Kempter spent the night there, while the other two descended with the porters to Camp IV.

Buhl set off for the summit alone and without additional oxygen at around 02:30, finally reaching it with his last reserves of strength at around 19:00. As proof of his ascent, he left his ice axe and the [Pakistani flag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flag_of_Pakistan "Flag of Pakistan") at the summit. Kempter, who had set off an hour later, was forced to turn back after a bout of weakness at an altitude of around 7,400 m (24,278 ft) on the plateau at the Silbersattel. He returned to Camp V, where he waited with Frauenberger and Ertl, who had climbed back up, for Buhl to return.

Buhl spent the following night alone, about 1.2 km (4,000 feet) higher up than Camp V. He survived the night at an altitude of almost 8,000 m (26,200 ft) without bivouac equipment only because of unusually favourable weather.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-AJ-buhl-14) However, he suffered [frostbite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frostbite "Frostbite") on two of his toes and still had most of the descent ahead of him. At times he fell into a dangerous state of apathy and suffered perceptual illusions, which he combated with [Pervitin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pervitin "Pervitin").

After 41 hours and in states of extreme exhaustion and dehydration, Buhl arrived back at Camp V, where hopes of his return had already begun to fade.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-AJ-buhl-14) In the days that followed, he also completed the descent to the main camp unaided, arriving there on 7 July. Here it turned out that the big toe and part of the second toe on his right foot could not be saved and had to be amputated.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-16) He therefore had to be carried on the rest of the return march.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Hans Ertl made a documentary film called _Nanga Parbat_ about this expedition.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-17)

A dispute arose between Herrligkoffer and Buhl after the expedition due to Herrligkoffer's authoritarian leadership and Buhl's refusal to follow orders without question. Expedition members had contractually ceded sole exploitation rights over the expedition's results to Herrligkoffer, and his rigorous enforcement of this clause led to a protracted legal dispute with Buhl and Hans Ertl.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-18)

Buhl is the only mountaineer to have made the first ascent of an [eight-thousander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eight-thousander "Eight-thousander") solo, achieved on his first visit to the [Greater Ranges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roof_of_the_World "Roof of the World").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-Isserman-19) His monumental efforts, which included spending the night standing untethered on a tiny pedestal, too small to crouch on, at the edge of a 60-degree ice slope, have become mountaineering legend, described by [Bonington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Bonington "Chris Bonington") as "a magnificent achievement".[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-Quest-20)

In 1999, Buhl's ice axe, which had been left behind on the summit, was found by a Japanese expedition and returned to his widow.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-21)

### Broad Peak

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hermann_Buhl&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Broad Peak")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cc/Buhl_Bergland-Wimpel.jpg/250px-Buhl_Bergland-Wimpel.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Buhl_Bergland-Wimpel.jpg)

Hermann Buhl memorial plaque in the August-Schuster-Haus with original pennant

[Fritz Wintersteller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fritz_Wintersteller "Fritz Wintersteller") and [Kurt Diemberger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurt_Diemberger "Kurt Diemberger") reached the forepeak (8,030 m (26,345 ft)) on 29 May 1957, during the course of the Austrian expedition led by [Marcus Schmuck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Schmuck "Marcus Schmuck"). However, it was a few days later, between 8 and 9 June, that Wintersteller, Schmuck, Diemberger, and Buhl reached the true summit of [Broad Peak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broad_Peak "Broad Peak") (8,051 m (26,414 ft)) and achieved the first successful ascent of the mountain. Buhl approached the summit in the twilight, at around 18:30.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-DiemBroad-22) The ascent was accomplished without the aid of supplemental oxygen, high-altitude porters or base camp support.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-DiemBroad-22) The original pennant bearing the Bergland section's emblem, which appears in Buhl's summit photo, is on display in the restaurant of the [August-Schuster-Haus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/August-Schuster-Haus?action=edit&redlink=1 "August-Schuster-Haus (page does not exist)") in [Garmisch-Partenkirchen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garmisch-Partenkirchen "Garmisch-Partenkirchen"). This summit photo and Buhl's last letter to his comrades from Bergland can be found in the commemorative publication for the 50th anniversary of the Bergland section in 1958.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-23)

### Chogolisa

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hermann_Buhl&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Chogolisa")]

Just a few weeks after the successful [first ascent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_ascent "First ascent") of Broad Peak, Buhl and Diemberger made an attempt on nearby, unclimbed [Chogolisa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chogolisa "Chogolisa") (7,665 m (25,148 ft)) in [Alpine style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpine_style "Alpine style").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-24) Buhl lost his way in an unexpected snowstorm on the southeast ridge, near the summit of Chogolisa II (7,654 m (25,112 ft); also known as Bride Peak), and walked over a huge [cornice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornice_(climbing) "Cornice (climbing)") overhanging the mountain's north face, subsequently triggering an [avalanche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avalanche "Avalanche") that hurled him down the face.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-DiemBroad-22) His body could not be recovered and remains in the ice. After losing sight of Buhl in the storm, Diemberger, who was climbing with him, found his footsteps leading to a fresh breach in the cornice.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-DiemBroad-22)

## Legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hermann_Buhl&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Legacy")]

Buhl was the first person to climb an eight-thousander on the final section alone and without additional oxygen.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-Isserman-19) Austrian sports journalists voted him "[Sportsman of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austrian_Sports_Personality_of_the_Year "Austrian Sports Personality of the Year") 1953" on 21 January 1954.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-25)

Because of his prominent first ascents in the Alps and the [Karakoram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karakoram "Karakoram"), [Reinhold Messner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinhold_Messner "Reinhold Messner") has described Buhl as the best all-round mountaineer of his time.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-26) His solo ascent of Nanga Parbat was made against explicit orders. This sat uneasily with the nationalist framing under which the West German and Austrian public had followed the expedition, since the mountain had been styled as a "German fate-mountain" (_Schicksalsberg der Deutschen_) after earlier German expeditions in the 1930s.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-27) Rather than mounting heavily equipped, large-scale expeditions, he preferred travelling light, climbing fast, and forgoing supplemental oxygen. He was also a role model for climbers of younger generations, including [Reinhold Messner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinhold_Messner "Reinhold Messner")[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-Buhllaw-13) and [Peter Habeler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Habeler "Peter Habeler"), who cited Buhl as one of his inspirations.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-28)

In 2006, the Austrian mountaineer and alpine historian [Markus Kronthaler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markus_Kronthaler "Markus Kronthaler") died from exhaustion during the descent after reaching the summit of Broad Peak.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-29)

### Honoring

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hermann_Buhl&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Honoring")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/58/Hermann-Buhl_Platz_Innsbruck_2023-09-25_01.jpg/250px-Hermann-Buhl_Platz_Innsbruck_2023-09-25_01.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hermann-Buhl_Platz_Innsbruck_2023-09-25_01.jpg)

Hermann-Buhl Platz Innsbruck

On 24 September 2012, the previously unnamed square in front of the [Hungerburgbahn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungerburgbahn "Hungerburgbahn") mountain station in Innsbruck was named Hermann-Buhl-Platz after Hermann Buhl.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-31)

His expedition to Nanga Parbat was dramatized by [Donald Shebib](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Shebib "Donald Shebib") in the 1986 film _[The Climb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Climb\_(1986\_film) "The Climb (1986 film)")_, based in part on Buhl's own writings about the expedition and starring [Bruce Greenwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Greenwood "Bruce Greenwood") as Buhl.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Buhl#cite_note-groen-32)

# HERCULES WATCHES

Switzerland based Hercules Watches Company produces mechanical timepieces inspired by mountaineering. Available in hand-wound and automatic versions, these robust and reliable timekeepers blend Alpinism and exquisite craftsmanship.

Watches

![Image 1: HERCULES WATCHES](https://i0.wp.com/masterhorologer.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/HERCULES-WATCHES-1.jpg?resize=600%2C400&ssl=1)

In 1953, an Austrian mountaineer called Hermann Buhl became the first person to climb the Nanga Parbat mountain 8’126 M. Around his wrist: a Hercules watch.

### History of Hercules Watches

Watchmaker Robert Pfaff, whose family had already manufactured watches in Pforzheim in the 1920s and 1930s, took on co-partner Robert Henzi around 1946, and a new company was founded.

Discover more

Luxury Goods

watchmaking

Hiking & Camping

In 1952, Henzi & Pfaff employed a little more than 200 people. They opened a manufacture in Stein, Germany. Henzi & Pfaff developed a very successful marketing strategy. When in 1953, a German-Austrian mountaineering group was supposed to climb the Himalayan summit Nanga Parbat for the first time. Henzi & Pfaff equipped the group with their Hercules timepieces.

The triumphant ascent and the worldwide attention of the expedition were marketed very effectively by Henzi & Pfaff. As a result, Henzi & Pfaff started further expeditions with watches and thus developed the image of reliable, robust, and at the same time, sporty watches.

Hiking & Camping

Buhl left the base camp at 02:00 on the 3rd of July in 1953. Around 19:00, he reached the top and became the first person to climb an 8’000-er alone. He couldn’t return to the base-camp and spent the night on a small ledge with only space to stand up. At the end of the following day, he reached one of the base camps. The other members of the expedition assumed that he had died already. Buhl became a legendary climber. Several books have been written about him, and two movies have been made.

### Revival

In 2022, the brand made a comeback with an exclusive series of Swiss made watches based on the original pieces that went up the mountain.

![Image 2: HERCULES WATCHES](https://i0.wp.com/masterhorologer.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/HERCULES-WATCHES-2.jpg?resize=600%2C400&ssl=1)

On May 21st, 2023, renowned mountain climber and polar ski guide, Ryan Waters successfully ascended Mount Everest, 8,848.86 m (29,031 ft 8+1⁄2 in).

He climbed to the top of the world with a Hercules Watch based on the original timepiece that went up with Hermann Buhl, who climbed the Nanga Parbat in 1953.

In 2023, the luxury-alpinist brand released the new [**Natural Ice Wonders**](https://masterhorologer.com/2023/10/13/hercules-watches-natural-ice-wonders-collection/)collection.

# To the Top of Everest with the HP Hercules Hand-Wound Double Barrelled

## Based on the 1953 original, it not only looks Everest-ready, but this actual watch went there!

30/09/2025|[By Robin Nooy](https://monochrome-watches.com/author/robin/ "Robin Nooy")| 5 min read |

![Image 6](https://monochrome-watches.com/app/uploads/2025/09/HP-Hercules-Hand-Wound-Double-Barreled-Climbed-mount-everest-review-1.jpg)

**Have you ever, like me, wondered what it would feel like to stand on the top of [Mount Everest](https://monochrome-watches.com/interview-adrian-ballinger-climbing-everest-no-oxygen-favre-leuba-bivouac-9000/)? Reaching Earth’s highest summit must be an exhilarating experience, to say the least. Although the climb to the top is heavily commercialised these days, it’s still a crazy and highly daunting adventure, and one that claims multiple lives every year. Regardless, the hunger for what is essentially [the ultimate adventure is felt by many](https://monochrome-watches.com/cory-richards-his-attempt-to-blaze-a-new-route-up-mount-everest-and-a-vacheron-constantin-overseas-prototype/), including watchmakers. Take HP Hercules, for instance, who in 1953 made it to the top of Nanga Parbat, the ninth highest peak on the planet. After its revival in 2022, the brand launched a historically inspired watch that once again captures the essence of high-altitude mountaineering. We take a closer look at the HP Hercules Hand-Wound Double Barrelled, a watch that not too long ago made another historical climb!**

[![Image 7](https://monochrome-watches.com/app/themes/monochromewatches/dist/images/image_placeholder.svg)](https://monochrome-watches.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/HP-Hercules-Watches-historic-image.jpg)

The history of HP Hercules Watches dates back a long way, with the company originating under the name Henzi & Pfaff in the 1920s. Shortly after World War II, it resumed manufacturing watch movements, and by the 1950s, it was selling watches under the name HP Hercules. In 1953, the company hit proverbial marketing gold, as one of their watches accompanied Austrian mountaineer Hermann Buhl on the first successful climb to the top of Nanga Parbat, one of the highest mountains on Earth. Prior to that, 31 climbers lost their lives trying to reach the 8,126m summit, which became known as ‘The Killer Mountain’ because of it. What’s perhaps even more impressive is the fact that Buhl managed to do it solo!

[![Image 9: HP Hercules Hand-Wound Double Barreled Ryan Waters on mount everest - 2](https://monochrome-watches.com/app/themes/monochromewatches/dist/images/image_placeholder.svg)](https://monochrome-watches.com/app/uploads/2025/09/HP-Hercules-Hand-Wound-Double-Barreled-Ryan-Waters-on-mount-everest-2.jpeg)

[![Image 11: HP Hercules Hand-Wound Double Barreled Ryan Waters on mount everest - 1](https://monochrome-watches.com/app/themes/monochromewatches/dist/images/image_placeholder.svg)](https://monochrome-watches.com/app/uploads/2025/09/HP-Hercules-Hand-Wound-Double-Barreled-Ryan-Waters-on-mount-everest-1.jpg)

Now, seventy years later, HP Hercules has been brought back to life thanks to[Adriaan Trampe](https://monochrome-watches.com/eza-watches-sealander-dutch-brand/), a Dutch watchmaker who previously worked with[Diederik van Golen](https://monochrome-watches.com/category/volan-watches/) under the name[EZA Watches](https://monochrome-watches.com/category/eza-watches/). With history in mind, HP Hercules returned to that pivotal 1953 watch for its first collection, which comes in a hand-wound or micro-rotor automatic configuration. And to come full circle, Ryan Waters, an experienced explorer and “Grand Slam” adventurer (reaching the North Pole, South Pole and the highest peak on each continent), took one to the top of Mount Everest without any issue. That very watch, battle-scared and all, is the one you see in these images.

[![Image 13](https://monochrome-watches.com/app/themes/monochromewatches/dist/images/image_placeholder.svg)](https://monochrome-watches.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/HP-Hercules-Hand-Wound-Double-Barreled-Climbed-mount-everest-review-9.jpg)

As it takes after the original watch worn by Buhl in 1953, the HP Hercules Hand-Wound Double Barrelled looks fairly straightforward. However, as you’ll discover by reading on, it packs a surprising bit of character! The case is a three-part construction, measuring 40mm in diameter and 9.4mm in height. With a lug-to-lug of a relatively short 46mm, the fully polished watch wears very nicely on pretty much any wrist. The lugs have a subtly shaped profile to separate them from the case a bit, and the large yet flat crown is easy to grip and manipulate. There’s a sapphire crystal on both the front and back of the watch, and it is water-resistant to 100m.

[![Image 15: HP Hercules Hand-Wound Double Barreled - Climbed mount everest - review - 8](https://monochrome-watches.com/app/themes/monochromewatches/dist/images/image_placeholder.svg)](https://monochrome-watches.com/app/uploads/2025/09/HP-Hercules-Hand-Wound-Double-Barreled-Climbed-mount-everest-review-8.jpg)

[![Image 17: HP Hercules Hand-Wound Double Barreled - Climbed mount everest - review - 7](https://monochrome-watches.com/app/themes/monochromewatches/dist/images/image_placeholder.svg)](https://monochrome-watches.com/app/uploads/2025/09/HP-Hercules-Hand-Wound-Double-Barreled-Climbed-mount-everest-review-7.jpg)

Drawing inspiration from nature, the dial features a snowflake-like texture. Our review watch was the Ice Blue version, as worn by Ryan Waters to the top of Mount Everest, but it also comes in Snow White, Ice Green or Ice Pink. These colours aren’t just random, but tied to natural phenomena in glacial structures. The white and blue dials speak for themselves, of course, but the green and pink come from algae found in snowy or icy regions. The overall design of the dial is fairly simple, as it’s inspired by the 1953 original. The shape of the hands is identical as well, although it now relies on modern Super-LumiNova for the luminous inserts. The central second hand is lacquered in red to stand out.

[![Image 19](https://monochrome-watches.com/app/themes/monochromewatches/dist/images/image_placeholder.svg)](https://monochrome-watches.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/HP-Hercules-Hand-Wound-Double-Barreled-Climbed-mount-everest-review-2.jpg)

The applied markers and numerals are polished, providing an equally strong contrast against the backdrop of the base dial as the hands. On the outer perimeter, there’s a minute track with small luminous squares. Further details include the applied logo with the brand name just below it, in black, and the printed caption in the bottom, indicating that it comes with a chronometer-certified movement. Again, some might argue the dial is a bit empty, but I would disagree, as the texture adds a lot of life, plus the fact that it takes after a historic Hercules watch after all.

[![Image 21](https://monochrome-watches.com/app/themes/monochromewatches/dist/images/image_placeholder.svg)](https://monochrome-watches.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/HP-Hercules-Hand-Wound-Double-Barreled-Climbed-mount-everest-review-3.jpg)

Inside the Hand-Wound Double Barelled is a movement made in close collaboration with Manufacture Horlogère Vallée de Joux, in Le Sentier, Switzerland. And for those that might detect a sense of familiarity, it’s indeed similar to some of [the Technotime movements we’ve seen in the past](https://monochrome-watches.com/search/technotime/). The design and rights of that movement are now owned by MHVJ (or Manufacture Horlogère Vallée de Joux SA, part of the Festina Group), which has then changed the anchor, escape wheel, balance and balance spring to improve its accuracy and receive Chronometer certification.

[![Image 23: HP Hercules Hand-Wound Double Barreled - Climbed mount everest - review - 5](https://monochrome-watches.com/app/themes/monochromewatches/dist/images/image_placeholder.svg)](https://monochrome-watches.com/app/uploads/2025/09/HP-Hercules-Hand-Wound-Double-Barreled-Climbed-mount-everest-review-5.jpg)

[![Image 25: HP Hercules Hand-Wound Double Barreled - Climbed mount everest - review - 6](https://monochrome-watches.com/app/themes/monochromewatches/dist/images/image_placeholder.svg)](https://monochrome-watches.com/app/uploads/2025/09/HP-Hercules-Hand-Wound-Double-Barreled-Climbed-mount-everest-review-6.jpg)

Covered by a sapphire crystal caseback, you get a full glimpse of the double-barrelled setup, the centre wheel, and the balance wheel and escapement. What also stands out are the contour lines on the bridges, similar to those found on a map. These are also filled with Super-LumiNova to make them stand out a touch more. The movement is also a certified chronometer, as [Timelab Geneva](https://monochrome-watches.com/search/timelab+geneve/) puts each movement through its rigorous testing procedure to make sure it performs as best as it can. Alternatively, there’s also a micro-rotor automatic version, in a similar design but with a lower power reserve of 70 hours (due to the fact that it has only one barrel).

[![Image 27](https://monochrome-watches.com/app/themes/monochromewatches/dist/images/image_placeholder.svg)](https://monochrome-watches.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/HP-Hercules-Hand-Wound-Double-Barreled-Climbed-mount-everest-review-4.jpg)

The HP Hercules Hand-Wound Double Barrelled comes on a calfskin or suede leather strap in grey or cognac as standard. Regardless, they are fitted with quick-release push pins to easily swap one out for another, plus a signed stainless steel pin buckle. The watches are made to order with a lead time of 4 to 6 weeks, which is partially due to the 21-day testing period by Timelab Genève. The price is set at **EUR 5,995**, which may sound like a hefty price for what looks like a fairly simple watch at first, but the design is coherent, and the overall quality is very good. The movement is solid, the watch wears nicely on the wrist, plus it comes packed with heritage.

For more information, please visit [HerculesWatches.com](https://herculeswatches.com/).

# To the Top of Everest with the HP Hercules Hand-Wound Double Barrelled

## Based on the 1953 original, it not only looks Everest-ready, but this actual watch went there!

30/09/2025|[By Robin Nooy](https://monochrome-watches.com/author/robin/ "Robin Nooy")| 5 min read |

![Image 6](https://monochrome-watches.com/app/uploads/2025/09/HP-Hercules-Hand-Wound-Double-Barreled-Climbed-mount-everest-review-1.jpg)

**Have you ever, like me, wondered what it would feel like to stand on the top of [Mount Everest](https://monochrome-watches.com/interview-adrian-ballinger-climbing-everest-no-oxygen-favre-leuba-bivouac-9000/)? Reaching Earth’s highest summit must be an exhilarating experience, to say the least. Although the climb to the top is heavily commercialised these days, it’s still a crazy and highly daunting adventure, and one that claims multiple lives every year. Regardless, the hunger for what is essentially [the ultimate adventure is felt by many](https://monochrome-watches.com/cory-richards-his-attempt-to-blaze-a-new-route-up-mount-everest-and-a-vacheron-constantin-overseas-prototype/), including watchmakers. Take HP Hercules, for instance, who in 1953 made it to the top of Nanga Parbat, the ninth highest peak on the planet. After its revival in 2022, the brand launched a historically inspired watch that once again captures the essence of high-altitude mountaineering. We take a closer look at the HP Hercules Hand-Wound Double Barrelled, a watch that not too long ago made another historical climb!**

[![Image 7](https://monochrome-watches.com/app/themes/monochromewatches/dist/images/image_placeholder.svg)](https://monochrome-watches.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/HP-Hercules-Watches-historic-image.jpg)

The history of HP Hercules Watches dates back a long way, with the company originating under the name Henzi & Pfaff in the 1920s. Shortly after World War II, it resumed manufacturing watch movements, and by the 1950s, it was selling watches under the name HP Hercules. In 1953, the company hit proverbial marketing gold, as one of their watches accompanied Austrian mountaineer Hermann Buhl on the first successful climb to the top of Nanga Parbat, one of the highest mountains on Earth. Prior to that, 31 climbers lost their lives trying to reach the 8,126m summit, which became known as ‘The Killer Mountain’ because of it. What’s perhaps even more impressive is the fact that Buhl managed to do it solo!

[![Image 11: HP Hercules Hand-Wound Double Barreled Ryan Waters on mount everest - 1](https://monochrome-watches.com/app/themes/monochromewatches/dist/images/image_placeholder.svg)](https://monochrome-watches.com/app/uploads/2025/09/HP-Hercules-Hand-Wound-Double-Barreled-Ryan-Waters-on-mount-everest-1.jpg)

Now, seventy years later, HP Hercules has been brought back to life thanks to[Adriaan Trampe](https://monochrome-watches.com/eza-watches-sealander-dutch-brand/), a Dutch watchmaker who previously worked with[Diederik van Golen](https://monochrome-watches.com/category/volan-watches/) under the name[EZA Watches](https://monochrome-watches.com/category/eza-watches/). With history in mind, HP Hercules returned to that pivotal 1953 watch for its first collection, which comes in a hand-wound or micro-rotor automatic configuration. And to come full circle, Ryan Waters, an experienced explorer and “Grand Slam” adventurer (reaching the North Pole, South Pole and the highest peak on each continent), took one to the top of Mount Everest without any issue. That very watch, battle-scared and all, is the one you see in these images.

[![Image 13](https://monochrome-watches.com/app/themes/monochromewatches/dist/images/image_placeholder.svg)](https://monochrome-watches.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/HP-Hercules-Hand-Wound-Double-Barreled-Climbed-mount-everest-review-9.jpg)

As it takes after the original watch worn by Buhl in 1953, the HP Hercules Hand-Wound Double Barrelled looks fairly straightforward. However, as you’ll discover by reading on, it packs a surprising bit of character! The case is a three-part construction, measuring 40mm in diameter and 9.4mm in height. With a lug-to-lug of a relatively short 46mm, the fully polished watch wears very nicely on pretty much any wrist. The lugs have a subtly shaped profile to separate them from the case a bit, and the large yet flat crown is easy to grip and manipulate. There’s a sapphire crystal on both the front and back of the watch, and it is water-resistant to 100m.

[![Image 15: HP Hercules Hand-Wound Double Barreled - Climbed mount everest - review - 8](https://monochrome-watches.com/app/themes/monochromewatches/dist/images/image_placeholder.svg)](https://monochrome-watches.com/app/uploads/2025/09/HP-Hercules-Hand-Wound-Double-Barreled-Climbed-mount-everest-review-8.jpg)

[![Image 17: HP Hercules Hand-Wound Double Barreled - Climbed mount everest - review - 7](https://monochrome-watches.com/app/themes/monochromewatches/dist/images/image_placeholder.svg)](https://monochrome-watches.com/app/uploads/2025/09/HP-Hercules-Hand-Wound-Double-Barreled-Climbed-mount-everest-review-7.jpg)

Drawing inspiration from nature, the dial features a snowflake-like texture. Our review watch was the Ice Blue version, as worn by Ryan Waters to the top of Mount Everest, but it also comes in Snow White, Ice Green or Ice Pink. These colours aren’t just random, but tied to natural phenomena in glacial structures. The white and blue dials speak for themselves, of course, but the green and pink come from algae found in snowy or icy regions. The overall design of the dial is fairly simple, as it’s inspired by the 1953 original. The shape of the hands is identical as well, although it now relies on modern Super-LumiNova for the luminous inserts. The central second hand is lacquered in red to stand out.

[![Image 19](https://monochrome-watches.com/app/themes/monochromewatches/dist/images/image_placeholder.svg)](https://monochrome-watches.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/HP-Hercules-Hand-Wound-Double-Barreled-Climbed-mount-everest-review-2.jpg)

The applied markers and numerals are polished, providing an equally strong contrast against the backdrop of the base dial as the hands. On the outer perimeter, there’s a minute track with small luminous squares. Further details include the applied logo with the brand name just below it, in black, and the printed caption in the bottom, indicating that it comes with a chronometer-certified movement. Again, some might argue the dial is a bit empty, but I would disagree, as the texture adds a lot of life, plus the fact that it takes after a historic Hercules watch after all.

[![Image 21](https://monochrome-watches.com/app/themes/monochromewatches/dist/images/image_placeholder.svg)](https://monochrome-watches.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/HP-Hercules-Hand-Wound-Double-Barreled-Climbed-mount-everest-review-3.jpg)

Inside the Hand-Wound Double Barelled is a movement made in close collaboration with Manufacture Horlogère Vallée de Joux, in Le Sentier, Switzerland. And for those that might detect a sense of familiarity, it’s indeed similar to some of [the Technotime movements we’ve seen in the past](https://monochrome-watches.com/search/technotime/). The design and rights of that movement are now owned by MHVJ (or Manufacture Horlogère Vallée de Joux SA, part of the Festina Group), which has then changed the anchor, escape wheel, balance and balance spring to improve its accuracy and receive Chronometer certification.

[![Image 23: HP Hercules Hand-Wound Double Barreled - Climbed mount everest - review - 5](https://monochrome-watches.com/app/themes/monochromewatches/dist/images/image_placeholder.svg)](https://monochrome-watches.com/app/uploads/2025/09/HP-Hercules-Hand-Wound-Double-Barreled-Climbed-mount-everest-review-5.jpg)

[![Image 25: HP Hercules Hand-Wound Double Barreled - Climbed mount everest - review - 6](https://monochrome-watches.com/app/themes/monochromewatches/dist/images/image_placeholder.svg)](https://monochrome-watches.com/app/uploads/2025/09/HP-Hercules-Hand-Wound-Double-Barreled-Climbed-mount-everest-review-6.jpg)

Covered by a sapphire crystal caseback, you get a full glimpse of the double-barrelled setup, the centre wheel, and the balance wheel and escapement. What also stands out are the contour lines on the bridges, similar to those found on a map. These are also filled with Super-LumiNova to make them stand out a touch more. The movement is also a certified chronometer, as [Timelab Geneva](https://monochrome-watches.com/search/timelab+geneve/) puts each movement through its rigorous testing procedure to make sure it performs as best as it can. Alternatively, there’s also a micro-rotor automatic version, in a similar design but with a lower power reserve of 70 hours (due to the fact that it has only one barrel).

[![Image 27](https://monochrome-watches.com/app/themes/monochromewatches/dist/images/image_placeholder.svg)](https://monochrome-watches.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/HP-Hercules-Hand-Wound-Double-Barreled-Climbed-mount-everest-review-4.jpg)

The HP Hercules Hand-Wound Double Barrelled comes on a calfskin or suede leather strap in grey or cognac as standard. Regardless, they are fitted with quick-release push pins to easily swap one out for another, plus a signed stainless steel pin buckle. The watches are made to order with a lead time of 4 to 6 weeks, which is partially due to the 21-day testing period by Timelab Genève. The price is set at **EUR 5,995**, which may sound like a hefty price for what looks like a fairly simple watch at first, but the design is coherent, and the overall quality is very good. The movement is solid, the watch wears nicely on the wrist, plus it comes packed with heritage.

For more information, please visit [HerculesWatches.com](https://herculeswatches.com/).

### Technical specifications – HP Hercules Hand-Wound Double Barrelled

**Case:** 40mm diameter x 9.4mm height - 46mm lug-to-lug - stainless steel case, polished - screwed bezel & caseback - sapphire crystal front & back - 100m water-resistant 

**Dial:** Ice Blue dial with snowflake-like texture (also available in white, green or pink) - applied polished faceted indices & numerals - pine-shaped hands with Super-LumiNova inserts - red-lacquered central seconds hand - printed minute track with luminous markers 

**Movement:** made in collaboration with Manufacture Horlogère Vallée de Joux - manual-winding - 30mm x 3.90mm - 26 jewels - 28,800vph - 120h power reserve - hours, minutes, seconds - mountain height lines with SLN - sunburst finishing - Chronometer Certified by TimeLab 

**Strap:** calf or suede leather strap with stainless steel pin buckle - custom straps available at no extra cost 

**Availability:** all watches made to order - 4 to 6 weeks lead time 

**Price:** EUR 5,995

**In 1953, an Austrian mountaineer named Hermann Buhl became the first person to climb the Nanga Parbat massif at 8 m. On his wrist: a Hercules watch.**

![Image 41](https://i0.wp.com/www.luxe-infinity.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/Nanga-Parbat.jpg?resize=1100%2C734&ssl=1)

![Image 42](https://i0.wp.com/www.luxe-infinity.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/Top-lid-box.jpg?resize=1100%2C388&ssl=1)

Watchmaker Robert Pfaff, whose family had already manufactured watches in Pforzheim in the 1920s and 1930s, joined forces with Robert Henzi in 1946 and a new company was founded. By 1952, Henzi & Pfaff employed just over 200 people. They opened a factory in Stein, Germany. At the same time, Henzi & Pfaff developed a highly effective marketing strategy. In 1953, a group of German-Austrian mountaineers was to climb the Himalayan peak Nanga Parbat for the first time. Henzi & Pfaff equipped the group with its Hercules watches. The triumphant ascent and the expedition's worldwide impact were very effectively marketed by Henzi & Pfaff. As a result, the company organized further expeditions with watches and thus developed its image as reliable, robust, and at the same time sporty watches.

![Image 43](https://i0.wp.com/www.luxe-infinity.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/HP2-snow-dial-5-.jpg?resize=1100%2C733&ssl=1)

Buhl left base camp at 02:00 a.m. on July 3, 1953. Around 19:8 p.m., he reached the summit and became the first person to climb 000 meters solo. He was unable to return to base camp and spent the night on a small ledge with only room to stand. By the end of the following day, he had reached one of the base camps. The other members of the expedition assumed he was already dead. Buhl became a legendary climber. Several books were written about him, and two films were made.

![Image 44](https://i0.wp.com/www.luxe-infinity.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/HP1-white-dial-2-.jpg?resize=1100%2C733&ssl=1)

Today, the brand returns with an exclusive series of watches inspired by the original pieces that climbed the mountain. The micro-rotor movement, specially designed for Hercules, took three years to develop. Each movement is tested by the Swiss Official Chronometer Testing Institute (COSC) in Switzerland and comes with an official certificate. The peaks of Nanga Parbat mountain can be seen engraved on the movement's bridges. Like the logo in the rotor, these lines are filled with SuperLuminova BRW9. This glows a bright blue, referencing the permafrost ice at the mountain's summit and creating a magical effect.

![Image 45](https://i0.wp.com/www.luxe-infinity.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/HP2-snow-dial.jpg?resize=1100%2C733&ssl=1)

The collection is now available for pre-order online. The first 15 pieces are numbered and are part of the first limited editions. Delivery begins in October 2022. The price of the watch is €5 for the white dial and €995 for the snow-effect dial.

**In 1953, an Austrian mountaineer named Hermann Buhl became the first person to climb the Nanga Parbat massif at 8 m. On his wrist: a Hercules watch.**

![Image 41](https://i0.wp.com/www.luxe-infinity.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/Nanga-Parbat.jpg?resize=1100%2C734&ssl=1)

![Image 42](https://i0.wp.com/www.luxe-infinity.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/Top-lid-box.jpg?resize=1100%2C388&ssl=1)

Watchmaker Robert Pfaff, whose family had already manufactured watches in Pforzheim in the 1920s and 1930s, joined forces with Robert Henzi in 1946 and a new company was founded. By 1952, Henzi & Pfaff employed just over 200 people. They opened a factory in Stein, Germany. At the same time, Henzi & Pfaff developed a highly effective marketing strategy. In 1953, a group of German-Austrian mountaineers was to climb the Himalayan peak Nanga Parbat for the first time. Henzi & Pfaff equipped the group with its Hercules watches. The triumphant ascent and the expedition's worldwide impact were very effectively marketed by Henzi & Pfaff. As a result, the company organized further expeditions with watches and thus developed its image as reliable, robust, and at the same time sporty watches.

![Image 43](https://i0.wp.com/www.luxe-infinity.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/HP2-snow-dial-5-.jpg?resize=1100%2C733&ssl=1)

Buhl left base camp at 02:00 a.m. on July 3, 1953. Around 19:8 p.m., he reached the summit and became the first person to climb 000 meters solo. He was unable to return to base camp and spent the night on a small ledge with only room to stand. By the end of the following day, he had reached one of the base camps. The other members of the expedition assumed he was already dead. Buhl became a legendary climber. Several books were written about him, and two films were made.

![Image 44](https://i0.wp.com/www.luxe-infinity.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/HP1-white-dial-2-.jpg?resize=1100%2C733&ssl=1)

Today, the brand returns with an exclusive series of watches inspired by the original pieces that climbed the mountain. The micro-rotor movement, specially designed for Hercules, took three years to develop. Each movement is tested by the Swiss Official Chronometer Testing Institute (COSC) in Switzerland and comes with an official certificate. The peaks of Nanga Parbat mountain can be seen engraved on the movement's bridges. Like the logo in the rotor, these lines are filled with SuperLuminova BRW9. This glows a bright blue, referencing the permafrost ice at the mountain's summit and creating a magical effect.

![Image 45](https://i0.wp.com/www.luxe-infinity.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/HP2-snow-dial.jpg?resize=1100%2C733&ssl=1)

The collection is now available for pre-order online. The first 15 pieces are numbered and are part of the first limited editions. Delivery begins in October 2022. The price of the watch is €5 for the white dial and €995 for the snow-effect dial.

# Nanga Parbat Death Rate: _why the Killer Mountain earns its name_

Long before it was ever climbed, Nanga Parbat had killed 31 people. It took the two worst mountaineering disasters of its era, a first ascent that has passed into legend, and a modern fatality rate still around one in five to build the reputation captured in its nickname. This is a clear-eyed look at the numbers behind the Killer Mountain: what the death rate actually is, how it has changed, why climbers die here, and the disasters that defined it.

By [Travis Ludlow](https://globalsummitguide.com/about/), Founder & Head of Research · With the Global Summit Guide Editorial Team · Safety review: Dawson Ludlow

Published Jul 18, 2026 · Last verified Jul 18, 2026 · ~9 min read

Death rates on 8,000ers are approximate and depend on how deaths and summits are counted and on the era measured, so every figure here is a considered estimate, not a fixed value. The short answer
## Roughly one climber dies for every five who summit.

Nanga Parbat’s modern fatality rate sits around **20 to 21 percent**, measured as deaths per summit, with something like **70 to 80 deaths against 400-plus ascents**. That makes it the **third-deadliest of the fourteen 8,000ers** by ratio, behind only [Annapurna I](https://globalsummitguide.com/annapurna-death-rate/) and [K2](https://globalsummitguide.com/k2-death-rate/). Unlike the crowded giants, this is a real, high per-climber risk, not a large toll spread thin over huge numbers.

## The _death rate_

A true high-risk mountain, where the ratio reflects real danger rather than sheer traffic.

Nanga Parbat, at 8,126 m (26,660 ft), is the ninth-highest mountain in the world and the western anchor of the Himalaya, standing alone above the Indus valley in Pakistan’s Gilgit-Baltistan. Its modern death rate is usually given as around 20 to 21 percent, meaning roughly one death for every five successful summits, with a cumulative toll of about 70 to 80 climbers against more than 400 ascents. That places it third among the 8,000ers by fatality ratio, behind Annapurna and K2. What makes the figure sobering is the context: where [Mont Blanc](https://globalsummitguide.com/mountains-mont-blanc-europe-italy-france/) or the [Matterhorn](https://globalsummitguide.com/mountains-matterhorn-switzerland/) accumulate large death tolls mainly because enormous numbers of people climb them, Nanga Parbat’s rate reflects a mountain that is lethal on any given attempt.

## Historical vs _modern_

Few mountains have a starker before-and-after than the Killer Mountain.

Nanga Parbat’s early record is almost without parallel. In the two decades before its first ascent, it killed 31 climbers without a single person reaching the top, a toll driven by two catastrophes covered below. Measured against that empty summit column, the pre-1953 death rate was effectively astronomical. The first ascent in 1953 broke the spell, and in the decades since, a growing number of successful climbs has brought the ratio down to its modern level of around 20 percent. That is a real improvement, but it is not safety: the mountain still kills at one of the highest rates of any 8,000er, because the hazards that caused those early disasters, above all avalanche and scale, remain exactly as they were.

**Reading the number.** A death rate of 20 percent does not mean any one climber has a one-in-five chance of dying on a given day. It is a cumulative deaths-to-summits ratio across the mountain’s history. But it does place Nanga Parbat firmly among the most dangerous peaks on Earth, and far above the roughly one percent rate of modern [Everest](https://globalsummitguide.com/mount-everest-nepal-tibet/).

## Why climbers _die_ here

The causes are stubborn, and several of them lie outside any climber’s control.

Avalanches are the leading killer on Nanga Parbat, and have been since the first expeditions probed the Rakhiot Face in the 1930s. Beyond that, the mountain stacks hazard on hazard. It is technically severe, ranked with K2 among the hardest of the 8,000ers on every route. Its scale is extraordinary: the Rupal Face on the south side rises around 4,600 m from base to summit, the highest mountain wall on Earth, and simply being on that terrain means enormous exposure and commitment. The weather is violent and fast-moving, the mountain is remote with limited rescue capacity, and much of the danger is objective, meaning a serac release or a slab avalanche can kill a strong, careful team that did everything right.

**⚠ Objective hazard cannot be climbed around**
The defining feature of Nanga Parbat’s danger is that skill only reduces part of it. Avalanche-swept slopes and the sheer scale of the faces expose climbers to risks that good decisions cannot fully remove. That is why the mountain has killed elite mountaineers, not only the unprepared, and why its rate has stayed high even as equipment and forecasting have improved.

## The defining _disasters_

Two pre-war catastrophes built the legend, and later tragedies deepened it.

1934

A storm trapped the German expedition high on the Rakhiot Face. Leader Willy Merkl, Uli Wieland, Willo Welzenbach and several Sherpas died in the retreat, one of the darkest episodes of the era.

1937

An avalanche swept the camp on the Rakhiot Face in the night, killing 16 climbers at once, seven Germans and nine Sherpas, among the worst single disasters in the history of mountaineering.

1953

Hermann Buhl reached the summit alone in a final push without oxygen or support, ending the mountain’s long unbeaten and deadly record with one of the sport’s greatest feats.

1970

Gunther Messner died descending the Diamir Face after he and his brother Reinhold completed the first ascent of the immense Rupal Face.

2016

Simone Moro, Alex Txikon and Muhammad Ali Sadpara made the first winter ascent, decades after the mountain’s first summer summit.

**A separate tragedy.** In 2013, militants attacked the Diamir Base Camp and killed ten climbers and a guide. This was an act of terrorism rather than a mountaineering accident, and it is not counted in the climbing fatality figures above, but it remains part of the mountain’s recent history and its perceived risk.

## How it _compares_

Nanga Parbat sits in the small, grim group of true high-fatality 8,000ers.

| Annapurna I | ~29-32% historical, ~13% modern | Avalanche and serac exposure |
| K2 | ~23% | Sustained technical, the Bottleneck serac |

The pattern is the one that runs through all mountain-fatality data: the deadliest peaks by ratio are the technical, avalanche-exposed giants that relatively few people attempt, while the mountains with the largest absolute death tolls tend to be the accessible, heavily-climbed ones. Nanga Parbat belongs firmly to the first group. **Reading the forecast.** Nanga Parbat is climbed mainly in the June to August summer window. Watch the 350 hPa wind (aim for sustained speeds under about 40 km/h for a summit push), summit temperatures, and fresh snow loading, which sharply raises avalanche danger on the Diamir and Rakhiot faces for a day or two after any storm. Always confirm current conditions with your operator and recent expedition reports.

## Nanga Parbat death rate _FAQ_

The questions people ask most.

### What is the death rate on Nanga Parbat?

Around 20 to 21 percent in the modern era, measured as deaths per summit, with roughly 70 to 80 deaths against more than 400 ascents. That makes it the third-deadliest 8,000er by ratio, behind Annapurna and K2, and it is often described as a one-in-five fatality rate.

### Why is it called the Killer Mountain?

Because before its 1953 first ascent it had killed 31 climbers without anyone summiting, including 10 in a 1934 storm and 16 in a single 1937 avalanche. The nickname, and the older Man Eater, reflect that catastrophic early record. Nanga Parbat itself means Naked Mountain.

### Is it more dangerous than Everest?

By per-climber risk, far more. Everest’s rate is now around 1 percent; Nanga Parbat’s is roughly 20 times higher. Everest’s larger absolute toll only reflects how many more people climb it.

### What kills climbers here?

Avalanches above all, plus extreme technical difficulty rivaling K2, the enormous Rupal Face, violent weather, and remoteness. Much of the hazard is objective, meaning it can kill even a strong, careful team.

### Has it got safer?

The catastrophic pre-1953 era has passed and more modern ascents have lowered the ratio, but at around 20 percent it remains one of the deadliest 8,000ers, because the core avalanche and scale hazards cannot be engineered away.

## Methodology, sources &_editorial standards_

How this analysis was built, and the limits of what it can promise.

### ![Image 5: 📋](https://s.w.org/images/core/emoji/17.0.2/svg/1f4cb.svg) Editorial standards & source verification

This Nanga Parbat death-rate analysis cross-checks fatality figures against multiple authoritative sources. The modern rate of roughly 20 percent, and the cumulative toll of 70 to 80 deaths against 400-plus summits, reflect Himalayan Database records and widely cited reporting; historical framing reflects the pre-1953 period when the mountain had many deaths and no summits. Both are accurate for their respective eras, and the change reflects more successful modern ascents rather than a fundamentally safer mountain.

The mountain’s hazards, the avalanche-prone Rakhiot and Diamir faces, the scale of the Rupal Face, and the technical difficulty on every route, remain as they have always been. Nanga Parbat has not become safe; it has been climbed more successfully in the modern era.

### ◆ Research-based, honestly framed

The Global Summit Guide editorial team has not climbed Nanga Parbat, and no one on the team has summited an 8,000-meter peak. This analysis synthesizes the most authoritative fatality records and primary mountaineering journalism rather than first-hand experience of the mountain. The team’s own high-altitude experience includes [Kilimanjaro](https://globalsummitguide.com/mountains/africa-tanzania-mount-kilimanjaro/) (5,895 m, summited by Dawson Ludlow), Pico de Orizaba (5,636 m), Iztaccihuatl, Rainier-class glaciated volcanoes, and Utah peaks, which informs our understanding of commercial high-altitude operations. Death-rate statistics, hazard analysis, and historical climb records are objective and verifiable across sources, which is what makes a research-based synthesis useful here.

# Nanga Parbat Death Rate: _why the Killer Mountain earns its name_

Long before it was ever climbed, Nanga Parbat had killed 31 people. It took the two worst mountaineering disasters of its era, a first ascent that has passed into legend, and a modern fatality rate still around one in five to build the reputation captured in its nickname. This is a clear-eyed look at the numbers behind the Killer Mountain: what the death rate actually is, how it has changed, why climbers die here, and the disasters that defined it.

By [Travis Ludlow](https://globalsummitguide.com/about/), Founder & Head of Research · With the Global Summit Guide Editorial Team · Safety review: Dawson Ludlow

Published Jul 18, 2026 · Last verified Jul 18, 2026 · ~9 min read

Death rates on 8,000ers are approximate and depend on how deaths and summits are counted and on the era measured, so every figure here is a considered estimate, not a fixed value. The short answer
## Roughly one climber dies for every five who summit.

Nanga Parbat’s modern fatality rate sits around **20 to 21 percent**, measured as deaths per summit, with something like **70 to 80 deaths against 400-plus ascents**. That makes it the **third-deadliest of the fourteen 8,000ers** by ratio, behind only [Annapurna I](https://globalsummitguide.com/annapurna-death-rate/) and [K2](https://globalsummitguide.com/k2-death-rate/). Unlike the crowded giants, this is a real, high per-climber risk, not a large toll spread thin over huge numbers.

## The _death rate_

A true high-risk mountain, where the ratio reflects real danger rather than sheer traffic.

Nanga Parbat, at 8,126 m (26,660 ft), is the ninth-highest mountain in the world and the western anchor of the Himalaya, standing alone above the Indus valley in Pakistan’s Gilgit-Baltistan. Its modern death rate is usually given as around 20 to 21 percent, meaning roughly one death for every five successful summits, with a cumulative toll of about 70 to 80 climbers against more than 400 ascents. That places it third among the 8,000ers by fatality ratio, behind Annapurna and K2. What makes the figure sobering is the context: where [Mont Blanc](https://globalsummitguide.com/mountains-mont-blanc-europe-italy-france/) or the [Matterhorn](https://globalsummitguide.com/mountains-matterhorn-switzerland/) accumulate large death tolls mainly because enormous numbers of people climb them, Nanga Parbat’s rate reflects a mountain that is lethal on any given attempt.

## Historical vs _modern_

Few mountains have a starker before-and-after than the Killer Mountain.

Nanga Parbat’s early record is almost without parallel. In the two decades before its first ascent, it killed 31 climbers without a single person reaching the top, a toll driven by two catastrophes covered below. Measured against that empty summit column, the pre-1953 death rate was effectively astronomical. The first ascent in 1953 broke the spell, and in the decades since, a growing number of successful climbs has brought the ratio down to its modern level of around 20 percent. That is a real improvement, but it is not safety: the mountain still kills at one of the highest rates of any 8,000er, because the hazards that caused those early disasters, above all avalanche and scale, remain exactly as they were.

**Reading the number.** A death rate of 20 percent does not mean any one climber has a one-in-five chance of dying on a given day. It is a cumulative deaths-to-summits ratio across the mountain’s history. But it does place Nanga Parbat firmly among the most dangerous peaks on Earth, and far above the roughly one percent rate of modern [Everest](https://globalsummitguide.com/mount-everest-nepal-tibet/).

## Why climbers _die_ here

The causes are stubborn, and several of them lie outside any climber’s control.

Avalanches are the leading killer on Nanga Parbat, and have been since the first expeditions probed the Rakhiot Face in the 1930s. Beyond that, the mountain stacks hazard on hazard. It is technically severe, ranked with K2 among the hardest of the 8,000ers on every route. Its scale is extraordinary: the Rupal Face on the south side rises around 4,600 m from base to summit, the highest mountain wall on Earth, and simply being on that terrain means enormous exposure and commitment. The weather is violent and fast-moving, the mountain is remote with limited rescue capacity, and much of the danger is objective, meaning a serac release or a slab avalanche can kill a strong, careful team that did everything right.

**⚠ Objective hazard cannot be climbed around**
The defining feature of Nanga Parbat’s danger is that skill only reduces part of it. Avalanche-swept slopes and the sheer scale of the faces expose climbers to risks that good decisions cannot fully remove. That is why the mountain has killed elite mountaineers, not only the unprepared, and why its rate has stayed high even as equipment and forecasting have improved.

## The defining _disasters_

Two pre-war catastrophes built the legend, and later tragedies deepened it.

1934

A storm trapped the German expedition high on the Rakhiot Face. Leader Willy Merkl, Uli Wieland, Willo Welzenbach and several Sherpas died in the retreat, one of the darkest episodes of the era.

1937

An avalanche swept the camp on the Rakhiot Face in the night, killing 16 climbers at once, seven Germans and nine Sherpas, among the worst single disasters in the history of mountaineering.

1953

Hermann Buhl reached the summit alone in a final push without oxygen or support, ending the mountain’s long unbeaten and deadly record with one of the sport’s greatest feats.

1970

Gunther Messner died descending the Diamir Face after he and his brother Reinhold completed the first ascent of the immense Rupal Face.

2016

Simone Moro, Alex Txikon and Muhammad Ali Sadpara made the first winter ascent, decades after the mountain’s first summer summit.

**A separate tragedy.** In 2013, militants attacked the Diamir Base Camp and killed ten climbers and a guide. This was an act of terrorism rather than a mountaineering accident, and it is not counted in the climbing fatality figures above, but it remains part of the mountain’s recent history and its perceived risk.

## How it _compares_

Nanga Parbat sits in the small, grim group of true high-fatality 8,000ers.

| K2 | ~23% | Sustained technical, the Bottleneck serac |

The pattern is the one that runs through all mountain-fatality data: the deadliest peaks by ratio are the technical, avalanche-exposed giants that relatively few people attempt, while the mountains with the largest absolute death tolls tend to be the accessible, heavily-climbed ones. Nanga Parbat belongs firmly to the first group. Watch the 350 hPa wind (aim for sustained speeds under about 40 km/h for a summit push), summit temperatures, and fresh snow loading, which sharply raises avalanche danger on the Diamir and Rakhiot faces for a day or two after any storm. ## Nanga Parbat death rate _FAQ_

The questions people ask most.

### What is the death rate on Nanga Parbat?

Around 20 to 21 percent in the modern era, measured as deaths per summit, with roughly 70 to 80 deaths against more than 400 ascents. That makes it the third-deadliest 8,000er by ratio, behind Annapurna and K2, and it is often described as a one-in-five fatality rate.

### Why is it called the Killer Mountain?

Because before its 1953 first ascent it had killed 31 climbers without anyone summiting, including 10 in a 1934 storm and 16 in a single 1937 avalanche. The nickname, and the older Man Eater, reflect that catastrophic early record. Nanga Parbat itself means Naked Mountain.

### Is it more dangerous than Everest?

By per-climber risk, far more. Everest’s rate is now around 1 percent; Nanga Parbat’s is roughly 20 times higher. Everest’s larger absolute toll only reflects how many more people climb it.

### What kills climbers here?

Avalanches above all, plus extreme technical difficulty rivaling K2, the enormous Rupal Face, violent weather, and remoteness. Much of the hazard is objective, meaning it can kill even a strong, careful team.

### Has it got safer?

The catastrophic pre-1953 era has passed and more modern ascents have lowered the ratio, but at around 20 percent it remains one of the deadliest 8,000ers, because the core avalanche and scale hazards cannot be engineered away.

## Methodology, sources &_editorial standards_

How this analysis was built, and the limits of what it can promise.

### ![Image 5: 📋](https://s.w.org/images/core/emoji/17.0.2/svg/1f4cb.svg) Editorial standards & source verification

This Nanga Parbat death-rate analysis cross-checks fatality figures against multiple authoritative sources. The modern rate of roughly 20 percent, and the cumulative toll of 70 to 80 deaths against 400-plus summits, reflect Himalayan Database records and widely cited reporting; historical framing reflects the pre-1953 period when the mountain had many deaths and no summits. Both are accurate for their respective eras, and the change reflects more successful modern ascents rather than a fundamentally safer mountain.

The mountain’s hazards, the avalanche-prone Rakhiot and Diamir faces, the scale of the Rupal Face, and the technical difficulty on every route, remain as they have always been. Nanga Parbat has not become safe; it has been climbed more successfully in the modern era.

### ◆ Research-based, honestly framed

The Global Summit Guide editorial team has not climbed Nanga Parbat, and no one on the team has summited an 8,000-meter peak. This analysis synthesizes the most authoritative fatality records and primary mountaineering journalism rather than first-hand experience of the mountain. The team’s own high-altitude experience includes [Kilimanjaro](https://globalsummitguide.com/mountains/africa-tanzania-mount-kilimanjaro/) (5,895 m, summited by Dawson Ludlow), Pico de Orizaba (5,636 m), Iztaccihuatl, Rainier-class glaciated volcanoes, and Utah peaks, which informs our understanding of commercial high-altitude operations. Death-rate statistics, hazard analysis, and historical climb records are objective and verifiable across sources, which is what makes a research-based synthesis useful here.

Nanga Parbat in Pakistan is called the “Killer Mountain” because it has historically had one of the highest fatality rates among the world’s 8,000-meter peaks. The figure of 64 climber deaths refers to historical climbing fatalities recorded before later years, not a single accident.

The main reasons so many climbers died include:

1. Extreme weather. 

Storms can develop within minutes, bringing hurricane-force winds, heavy snowfall, and temperatures well below freezing.

2. Frequent avalanches. 

Massive snow and ice avalanches have destroyed entire expeditions. One of the worst disasters occurred in 1934, when a storm and avalanche killed 10 members of a German expedition. 

3. Steep, technical terrain. 

Nanga Parbat’s famous Rupal Face rises about 4,600 meters from base to summit, making it one of the tallest mountain faces on Earth. The climbing is far more technically demanding than many Everest routes. 

4. High altitude. 

Above 8,000 meters lies the “death zone,” where oxygen levels are only about one-third of those at sea level. Climbers face exhaustion, altitude sickness, cerebral edema (HACE), and pulmonary edema (HAPE). 

5. Remoteness. 

Rescue operations are difficult because helicopters often cannot reach climbers in bad weather or at extreme altitude.

One important distinction: not all deaths on Nanga Parbat were caused by the mountain itself. In 2013, militants attacked the Diamir Base Camp and murdered 10 foreign climbers and one Pakistani guide in a terrorist assault. Those victims are included in some overall death statistics, but they were not mountaineering accidents. 

Although the historical figure of 64 deaths is often quoted, the total has increased over time as more expeditions have attempted the mountain. Nanga Parbat remains one of the most dangerous of the 14 eight-thousanders, earning its grim nickname through a combination of brutal terrain, unpredictable weather, and a long history of fatal expeditions.

Nanga Parbat in Pakistan is called the “Killer Mountain” because it has historically had one of the highest fatality rates among the world’s 8,000-meter peaks. The figure of 64 climber deaths refers to historical climbing fatalities recorded before later years, not a single accident.

The main reasons so many climbers died include:

1. Extreme weather. 

Storms can develop within minutes, bringing hurricane-force winds, heavy snowfall, and temperatures well below freezing.

2. Frequent avalanches. 

Massive snow and ice avalanches have destroyed entire expeditions. One of the worst disasters occurred in 1934, when a storm and avalanche killed 10 members of a German expedition. 

3. Steep, technical terrain. 

Nanga Parbat’s famous Rupal Face rises about 4,600 meters from base to summit, making it one of the tallest mountain faces on Earth. The climbing is far more technically demanding than many Everest routes. 

4. High altitude. 

Above 8,000 meters lies the “death zone,” where oxygen levels are only about one-third of those at sea level. Climbers face exhaustion, altitude sickness, cerebral edema (HACE), and pulmonary edema (HAPE). 

5. Remoteness. 

Rescue operations are difficult because helicopters often cannot reach climbers in bad weather or at extreme altitude.

One important distinction: not all deaths on Nanga Parbat were caused by the mountain itself. In 2013, militants attacked the Diamir Base Camp and murdered 10 foreign climbers and one Pakistani guide in a terrorist assault. Those victims are included in some overall death statistics, but they were not mountaineering accidents. 

Although the historical figure of 64 deaths is often quoted, the total has increased over time as more expeditions have attempted the mountain. Nanga Parbat remains one of the most dangerous of the 14 eight-thousanders, earning its grim nickname through a combination of brutal terrain, unpredictable weather, and a long history of fatal expeditions.

# A Climbing History of Nanga Parbat’s Deadly Rakhiot Face

July 7, 2025[Kris Annapurna](https://explorersweb.com/author/krisannapurna/ "Posts by Kris Annapurna")[History](https://explorersweb.com/category/history/) | [Nanga Parbat](https://explorersweb.com/category/nanga-parbat/)
